## Document_1

VPC (Virtual Port Channel) is a layer 2 technology that allows devices to connect to two Nexus switches simultaneously without creating loops, utilizing a PE link for traffic management. VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) is an overlay technology that encapsulates layer 2 frames into IP packets for transport over a layer 3 underlay network, typically arranged in a spine-leaf topology for scalability. When integrating VPC with VXLAN, it is crucial to maintain a PE link between Nexus pairs and configure loopback interfaces correctly, including a secondary IP that must be identical on both switches. Best practices include using different loopback interfaces for BGP peering and NVE interfaces, implementing a delay restore command for VPC recovery, and ensuring spanning tree is enabled with a 4-second hello time. Additionally, a backup routing SVI can be created to maintain connectivity in case of uplink failures, and specific commands may be required for certain switch models to ensure proper VXLAN functionality.

## Document_2

The video discusses configuring VXLAN with EVPN in a network topology involving two switches and multiple tenants. It begins with setting up the underlay network, including configuring OSPF and MTU sizes, and then moves on to the overlay configuration, enabling BGP for peering and setting up an anycast gateway. The configuration includes creating Layer 3 VNIs, associating them with VLANs, and setting up route distinguishers and targets for BGP. The use of head-end replication for multicast traffic is highlighted, along with ARP suppression to improve efficiency. The process of adding tenants and verifying configurations through various commands is also covered, demonstrating the separation of tenant traffic and the functionality of the network setup.

## Document_3

The video discusses the configuration of EVPN (Ethernet Virtual Private Network) for multiple tenants using VNI (Virtual Network Identifier) in a network environment. It details the creation of a new tenant with specific configurations, including the use of VLANs and enabling IP forwarding. The anti-cast gateway is set as the default gateway for external networks, and the process of verifying the configuration is outlined using various commands such as 'show BGP l2vpn evpn summary' to check BGP neighbors and 'show NVE vni' to view VNIs associated with the VTEP (Virtual Tunnel Endpoint). The commands for troubleshooting and verifying connectivity, including ARP suppression and MAC address learning through BGP, are also highlighted. The separation of tenant traffic is confirmed through ping tests, demonstrating successful isolation of resources between tenants.

## Document_4

The video discusses the configuration of VxLAN using data plane learning on Nexus 9000 series switches. It begins with a basic topology involving two switches, each with a VTEP interface and a routed link simulating the underlay network. The configuration includes associating VLAN 1000 with VNI 5000, enabling OSPF for the underlay, and configuring multicast for BUM traffic. Key steps include setting the MTU to accommodate VxLAN headers, configuring access ports, and establishing loopback interfaces for the VTEP IP address and rendezvous point. The NVE interface is configured to encapsulate traffic, and verification commands are provided to check the status of the VTEP and VNI configurations. The video emphasizes the simplicity of data plane learning compared to control plane learning, which will be covered in a subsequent part.

## Document_5

VXLAN is an overlay technology that creates tunnels over an IP underlay network, utilizing ingress and egress VTEPs for traffic encapsulation and delivery. Address learning can be achieved through data plane learning, which is similar to traditional Ethernet, or control plane learning using BGP to share MAC address information. Unicast and BUM (Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, and Multicast) traffic types require different handling methods, with multicast being the preferred solution for scalability. Control plane learning allows switches to learn MAC addresses before they are needed, enhancing efficiency and providing VTEP authentication through BGP. Integrated routing and bridging are supported with BGP EVPN, allowing for both Layer 2 and Layer 3 VNIs, facilitating features like anycast gateway for virtual machine mobility. The configuration of these technologies will be explored in subsequent parts of the series.

## Document_6

The video discusses the spine-leaf topology, a network architecture often associated with VXLAN, which consists of two layers: the spine layer and the leaf layer. In this architecture, leaf switches connect to spine switches, with no direct connections between spine switches or leaf switches, ensuring a consistent topology and avoiding unnecessary paths. Each leaf switch has a link to every spine switch, and all links are routed, requiring IP addresses at each end. This design allows for equal path lengths and quick recovery from link or switch failures using Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing. The spine-leaf architecture is particularly suited for data centers, facilitating east-west traffic patterns and scalability by simply adding more leaf switches or links. VXLAN operates as an overlay on this architecture, enabling device mobility without IP address changes. Border leaf switches provide connectivity to external networks, integrating firewalls and routers, and managing route redistribution between the overlay and core routing protocols.

## Document_7

VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) encapsulation is a technology that creates virtual Layer 2 segments called VNIs (VXLAN Network Identifiers) on top of a Layer 3 network. The process involves encapsulating an ordinary Ethernet frame, which may include a VLAN tag, into a VXLAN header that is added by a switch. The VXLAN header contains a 24-bit VNI, which allows for a large address space to support many VNIs. The encapsulated frame also includes UDP for transport, with a destination port of 4789 and a random source port for load balancing. An IP header and an Ethernet header are added for delivery, and upon reaching the destination, the headers are removed to deliver the original frame. The VXLAN header has reserved fields, with only one flag currently in use, and the additional headers can add around 50 bytes of overhead, necessitating the use of jumbo frames to avoid fragmentation and performance degradation.

## Document_8

VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) is an overlay technology that simplifies network design by allowing virtual machines to communicate across different VLANs without changing IP addresses. It uses a 24-bit segment identifier called a VNI (Virtual Network Identifier), allowing for approximately 16 million unique segments, which is significantly more than the 4,000 VLANs supported by traditional VLAN IDs. VXLAN operates over an underlay network that is entirely Layer 3, eliminating the need for spanning tree protocols and trunking. Traffic is encapsulated in UDP and IP headers for transmission, and VXLAN can be implemented on both hardware and software, including hypervisors like ESX or Hyper-V. Each VXLAN-enabled switch or router has a special interface called a VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint), which facilitates the connection between the overlay and underlay networks. query: What are the main configuration and operational factors to account for when deploying VPC together with VXLAN on Cisco Nexus switches in a spine-leaf architecture, particularly with respect to loopback interfaces, spanning tree protocol, BGP/EVPN integration, and encapsulation of traffic, to guarantee efficient operation, scalability, and fault tolerance?
answer:
Successfully integrating VPC and VXLAN on Cisco Nexus switches in a spine-leaf topology requires careful attention to several configuration and operational details:

1. Maintain a PE (peer) link between Nexus VPC pairs to prevent loops and ensure proper traffic management. Configure the peer-link as a port channel and use the keepalive link for VPC health, as outlined in VPC best practices.
2. Use different loopback interfaces for BGP peering and NVE (Network Virtualization Edge) interfaces. The NVE loopback should have a secondary IP that is identical on both switches in the VPC pair for VXLAN overlay functionality.
3. Enable and properly configure spanning tree with a 4-second hello time to ensure loop avoidance and fast convergence in the VPC domain.
4. Implement BGP EVPN for control-plane MAC address learning and separation of tenant traffic. Configure Layer 3 VNIs for routing between segments, associate VLANs with VNIs, and set up route distinguishers and targets for BGP.
5. Ensure the MTU is increased (jumbo frames) to accommodate VXLAN encapsulation overhead (~50 bytes) and prevent fragmentation.
6. Deploy the spine-leaf topology, where each leaf connects to every spine, to achieve scalability and ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) resiliency. VXLAN overlays this underlay for device mobility and tenant isolation.
7. Optionally, configure a backup routing SVI to maintain connectivity during uplink failures.

By following these guidelines, the network will support scalable, resilient multi-tenant overlays with seamless integration between VPC and VXLAN technologies.

## Document_2

The MAX BR1 Mk 2 can experience issues such as locking up and shutting off its access point, leading to a lack of DHCP connectivity when attempting to connect via the WAN port. A 'System Failed Integrity Check' message may appear, and performing a hard reset can temporarily resolve the issue. However, the problem may recur even after a factory reset, and disabling remote assistance has been noted to coincide with the router's failure to maintain functionality, requiring a power cycle to restore operation.

## Document_3

The Pepwave MAX BR1 Mk2 does not support NTP server features because it lacks a real-time chipset (RTC) with a battery. Therefore, it cannot function as an NTP time server for mobile devices connected to its access point.

## Document_4

The frequency bands that a modem covers are determined by its physical hardware characteristics and cannot be modified through software updates. To add support for a new frequency band, such as the lower frequency Sprint band, a new radio capable of tuning to that band would be necessary.

## Document_5

The BR1 MAX MK2 has two WiFi radios operating at 2.4GHz and 5GHz, and both radios are connected to both supplied dual-band antennas. This means that it is not possible to configure the device to have one radio exclusively handle WAN traffic while the other handles LAN traffic using separate antennas, as both radios share the same antenna connections.

## Document_6

After a fall, the RP-SMA connector for Antenna C on the Surf SOHO MK3 was found to be loose but still electrically connected. Testing showed that even with one antenna connected to any of the three connectors, Wi-Fi performance was acceptable. However, without any antenna, the device was unable to connect to a network, indicating that the antennas are essential for maintaining Wi-Fi connectivity.

## Document_7

The NTP time server functionality for the MAX BR-1 MK2 is not available in the production code but is included in version 8.1 RC1.

## Document_8

To configure the MAX BR-1 MK2 as an NTP time server, access the device's homepage and modify the URL to include 'support.cgi'. This will provide access to the necessary settings for NTP configuration.

## Document_9

If the RP-SMA connector for Antenna C on the Surf SOHO MK3 is loose, it may still be functional if it is connected to coaxial cable inside the device. query: What sequence of diagnostic and optimization steps should a technician follow when addressing slow WiFi and cellular performance issues on a Pepwave MAX BR1 Mini LTEA, taking into account hardware, configuration, signal quality, and firmware aspects?
answer: A technician should approach slow speeds on the Pepwave MAX BR1 Mini LTEA with a comprehensive diagnostic and optimization process. First, check the WiFi hardware, ensuring antennas are properly installed and not loose, and consider relocating the device to reduce interference and improve signal quality. Next, review WiFi configuration: try changing the wireless channel and adjusting transmit power (either increasing or decreasing), and set the channel width to 20/40MHz if using WiFi WAN. Since the device uses 2.4GHz 802.11n with one spatial stream, real-world speeds will be 40-45% of the PHY rate, so manage expectations accordingly. For cellular issues, verify both diversity and main antennas are installed, reposition them, and assess signal metrics like SINR, RSRQ, and Ec/Io; poor values suggest the need for a directional antenna or efforts to reduce local RF noise. Compare connection types: if the BR1 Mini connects only to 3G, speeds will be lower than phones using 4G LTE with the same SIM. Also, check for firmware updates (upgrade to at least 8.0.2) to resolve known issues and improve performance. Finally, avoid using the BR1 Mini for both WiFi WAN and LAN AP simultaneously, as its single-band, non-MIMO hardware will further reduce speeds; use a dedicated AP for LAN devices if possible.

## Document_1

The Peplink Balance 310 5G does not currently support the NetFlow feature, but a firmware fix is planned to enable this functionality. The fix is expected to be included in the next general availability (GA) firmware release.

## Document_2

To configure a Peplink Balance 310 5G to run traffic through SpeedFusion Cloud when the primary WAN connection goes down, set up the SpeedFusion Cloud connection to the nearest point of presence. Create an outbound policy named 'priority' with the wired WAN at the top of the list and SpeedFusion Cloud next, ensuring to tick the option to terminate sessions on link recovery before saving and applying the settings.

## Document_3

The Bandwidth Control feature on the PePLink Balance 710 is designed to manage traffic based on the source IP addresses or subnets of LAN and PPTP clients, allowing different bandwidth and traffic prioritization policies for user groups such as Manager, Staff, and Guest. It typically applies to internal (private) IP addresses rather than external (public) IP addresses, and does not restrict traffic to specific external sites. Currently, there is no functionality to shape traffic directed to particular external destinations, but this could be considered for future development.

## Document_4

The Peplink Balance 380 has a maximum limit of 50 concurrent OpenVPN connections. When this limit is reached, additional users attempting to connect will be blocked from establishing a VPN session.

## Document_5

The Peplink Balance 380 supports a maximum of 50 concurrent OpenVPN connections, as stated in the documentation. This limit is not just a recommendation; it is a hard-coded restriction. If a 51st VPN user attempts to connect, they will be blocked from establishing a VPN connection until one of the existing users disconnects, as the device cannot handle more than the specified number of concurrent connections.

## Document_6

When configuring a Peplink Balance 580 with two WAN connections for outbound DNS resolution, it is important to note that the secondary DNS server will only be used if the primary DNS server is unresponsive. The DNS traffic analysis may show internal NATted IP addresses, such as 192.168.17.198, instead of the queried external web addresses or IPs. To gain better visibility into DNS queries and responses across the network, setting up a syslog server can be beneficial.

## Document_7

When aggregating multiple internet connections using a Peplink Balance 580, the type of speed test conducted can significantly impact the results, as browser-based tests typically utilize a single session and may not effectively leverage all available WAN connections. Satellite connections often have high latency (around 800ms on KA band), which can hinder performance compared to DSL connections that have lower latency (20-50ms). For optimal performance, it is suggested to use the satellite link as a backup only, as it can negatively affect the overall speed and latency of the load-balanced connections.

## Document_8

When aggregating multiple internet connections using a Peplink Balance 580, the inclusion of a satellite connection with high latency can negatively impact overall speed. Specifically, the satellite connection should not be aggregated with DSL lines, as the high latency of the satellite connection can slow down the entire SpeedFusion VPN tunnel. It is recommended to combine satellite connections only with other satellite connections, while landlines can be effectively combined with cellular connections for better performance.

## Document_9

To route all SIP traffic through a T1 line with failover to a cable line on a Peplink Balance 580, outbound rules using IP addresses are recommended. Issues may arise when new devices connect to the network, as they can inadvertently use the T1 line, causing congestion for voice traffic. It is important to define outbound policies carefully and ensure that all devices are accounted for in the rules to maintain optimal performance.

## Document_10

To allow both internal and external access to an NVR for IP CCTV cameras using a Peplink Balance Core, a local DNS record can be set up to resolve the domain name (e.g., abc.domain.com) to the internal IP address (e.g., 192.168.50.10) when accessed from within the local network. This setup prevents the traffic from being routed externally and back to the NVR. Additionally, user devices should be configured to obtain DHCP IP addresses from the Balance Core, which will serve as the local DNS server.

## Document_11

To establish a backup connection for Offices B and C in the event of an MPLS failure, a Peplink Balance can be installed in both offices with ADSL lines connected for redundancy. A PepVPN can be set up from Offices B and C to HQ over the MPLS connection, but it is also possible to create a PepVPN from Offices B and C to Office A, which would then route traffic to HQ via the existing PepVPN. Additionally, it is feasible to configure the Peplink Balance in Offices B and C to failover to the ADSL lines and utilize a PepVPN when the MPLS connection is down, allowing for continued operation during outages.

## Document_12

The Peplink Balance series of routers, such as the Balance 30, offers comprehensive bandwidth monitoring features that allow users to track data usage across all WAN connections, including 3G, 4G, cable, and DSL. Users can view real-time data statistics, including total download and upload amounts, and analyze data spikes through graphical representations. The system provides daily and monthly overviews of data consumption, enabling users to identify specific devices or IP addresses that may be consuming excessive data. Additionally, the routers support seamless failover between connections and allow users to set data usage limits to prevent overage charges, particularly useful in usage-based billing scenarios. Notifications can be configured to alert users when operating on more expensive connections, and quality of service settings can be adjusted to prioritize bandwidth allocation based on individual user needs.

## Document_13

The Peplink Balance 310 5G modem is designed for branch offices and rural home users, featuring dual modems: a primary 5G modem with a theoretical maximum download speed of 4 Gbps and a secondary Category 12 modem with a maximum download speed of 600 Mbps. It supports up to four SIM cards (two for each modem) and includes five gigabit LAN ports, two SFP slots for fiber connections, and a USB port for adding a third cellular modem. The device is capable of SpeedFusion technology to bond multiple internet connections, making it suitable for failover scenarios. It does not have built-in Wi-Fi but can control external Wi-Fi access points, allowing for extensive wireless network setups. The modem supports a maximum throughput of 1 Gbps and can handle up to 600 Mbps for unencrypted VPN tunnels and 500 Mbps for encrypted tunnels. Additionally, it features a locking power connector to prevent accidental disconnection and is equipped with six cellular antennas for optimal connectivity.

## Document_14

The Balance 310 5G from Peplink features antennas capable of operating up to 2.7 GHz, providing four connections for a 5G modem and two for a category 12 modem. It includes a 60-watt power supply at 12 volts, which requires appropriate gauge wiring for mobile applications. While the device does not have built-in Wi-Fi, it supports the integration of Peplink wireless access points, allowing for automatic provisioning and management of multiple access points under a single SSID. The router has a maximum throughput of one gigabit and supports PepVPN with up to 600 megabits for unencrypted tunnels and 500 megabits for encrypted tunnels using 256-bit encryption. This makes it suitable for both high-speed internet access and secure site-to-site connectivity.

## Document_15

When configuring a Peplink Balance 580 with two WAN connections, it is important to set the DNS servers correctly for outbound DNS resolution. If a secondary DNS server is used, issues may arise where the DNS queries do not return expected results, potentially due to misconfigurations or external factors such as ISP redirection. In this case, the logs showed an unexpected IP address, indicating a possible issue with hostname resolution or DNS server order. Reversing the DNS server order might help in troubleshooting the issue, and contacting Peplink support for further diagnostics may be necessary.

## Document_16

To optimize the performance of a Peplink Balance 580 when aggregating multiple internet connections, outbound policy settings such as Weighted Balance can be defined to effectively load balance traffic across the 5 WAN connections. This approach can help manage the differing speeds and characteristics of DSL and satellite connections, potentially allowing for more efficient use of available bandwidth.

## Document_17

The user is running a Peplink Balance 580 to aggregate five internet connections: one satellite connection with 10 Mbps upload/download and four Bell DSL lines that combine for 20 Mbps download and 1 Mbps upload. The user has observed that disabling the DSL lines sometimes results in better connection speeds than when they are enabled. The user experiences inconsistent performance, noting that they cannot achieve full speeds through the Peplink device, while direct connection to the satellite provides the expected 10 Mbps speeds.

## Document_18

To ensure that SIP traffic is routed through a T1 line with failover to cable lines on a Peplink Balance 580, it is recommended to dedicate a VLAN for the Voice network. The outbound policy should source from the voice network and target trusted host networks, using UDP or TCP protocols. The algorithm should be set to priority for the circuits, avoiding load balancing for voice traffic to prevent issues such as one-way audio or registration problems during calls.

## Document_19

To set up a backup connection for Offices B and C in case the MPLS link to Office A goes down, a Peplink Balance can be installed in both offices with ADSL lines connected for backup. By enabling expert mode under outbound policies and defining the remote ends network under destination using the Priority algorithm, the MPLS link can be set as the top connection priority, while the PepVPN over ADSL lines can be set as the secondary option. This configuration ensures that all traffic is routed through MPLS unless it fails, at which point traffic will automatically switch to the PepVPN connection.

query: Which procedures and troubleshooting measures should be followed for updating firmware and AP firmware packs on a Balance One Core, particularly in scenarios where the automatic update does not succeed or the AP firmware pack fails to download or gets stuck?
answer:
To update the firmware on a Balance One Core, first try the online update via the System > Firmware section of the admin interface. If this fails or does not detect the latest version, consider using InControl2 for firmware management or manually entering the direct firmware URL using the 'Custom' option. For instance, firmware version 6.3.1 can be manually installed by entering its direct download link. If you experience timeouts or slow connections during manual upgrade, it may be due to unreliable firmware update features or slow network speeds.

For AP firmware packs, ensure you are uploading the firmware pack (not the standard AP firmware) via the AP controller toolbox. If the download or installation stalls (such as a spinning progress indicator), try deleting older firmware versions before attempting to download again. This issue may be due to bugs in certain firmware versions, so upgrading to the latest Balance One Core firmware can help resolve it. If multiple attempts fail, the issue may resolve itself after repeated tries, as observed in previous firmware releases.

query: What are the primary reasons and recommended diagnostic actions for experiencing slow download speeds with a Peplink Balance 20 router, particularly in cases where the ISP provides a connection that exceeds the router’s specified throughput?
answer: The most common cause of low download speeds on the Peplink Balance 20 router is hitting its hardware throughput limit, which can be 100 Mbps or 150 Mbps depending on the hardware revision and firmware version. If your ISP connection is faster, this hardware cap will bottleneck your speed. During large downloads or high traffic, the Balance 20 may become unresponsive or show high CPU usage, particularly if the WAN connection is much faster than the router can process. Other factors that can contribute to low speeds include misconfigured WAN interface port speed or duplex settings, improper MTU size (especially for DSL), suboptimal outbound policies, bandwidth limits set in the router, and the presence of managed switches or additional routing hops that add latency. To troubleshoot, verify your router’s hardware revision and firmware version to confirm its throughput rating; test your connection by bypassing the router to isolate the issue; check and adjust WAN interface settings (such as fixed port speed/duplex and MTU); ensure there are no unnecessary bandwidth limits or group reservations; and consider using features like DSL optimization or bufferbloat mitigation. If your needs exceed the Balance 20’s capabilities, upgrading to a higher-throughput model such as the Balance One or 20X is recommended.

The overflow algorithm in WAN connections operates by redirecting traffic from the primary WAN interface to a secondary WAN when the primary reaches a specified bandwidth threshold, typically set at 90% of its capacity. For example, if a fiber circuit on WAN 1 is configured for 100/100 Mbps and reaches 90% utilization, traffic will overflow to the next WAN in the outbound policy. This is particularly useful in scenarios with limited bandwidth, such as using a T1 line for VoIP phones, where traffic can overflow to a less stable ADSL circuit when the T1 reaches its capacity.

The satellite connection has a maximum traffic flow of 1Mb/s but guarantees only 100 Kb/s for downlink and 19.2 Kb/s for uplink. The user is seeking advice on the best algorithm to set for managing these WAN connections effectively, considering the fluctuating availability of bandwidth.

query: In what way do the Peplink Balance 210 and above models provide inbound load balancing along with redundancy and failover capabilities, and which DNS settings and necessary preconditions must be met to guarantee uninterrupted service if a WAN connection goes down?
answer: Peplink Balance 210 and higher models have a built-in authoritative DNS server that enables inbound load balancing by distributing inbound traffic across multiple WAN links. The DNS server manages DNS records (such as A, MX, and PTR) and responds to queries with the IP addresses of available WAN links. If one WAN link fails, the device automatically stops advertising the down link and responds only with IPs of live WANs, ensuring continuous connectivity and failover without IP changes or disconnections. For this functionality, each ISP connection must have a static (fixed) IP address, and DNS records at the domain registrar must be updated to delegate authority or point to the Peplink device. The setup can be managed entirely on the Peplink device, removing the need for third-party DNS servers. Proper configuration of these DNS records and static IPs is essential for seamless failover and redundancy.

query: What could cause a user to see much lower bandwidth than anticipated when combining several LTE WAN links, despite each LTE connection individually delivering good performance on separate devices?
answer: A user may experience lower than expected bandwidth when bonding multiple LTE WAN connections with SpeedFusion due to several factors. First, bonding introduces overhead from additional headers, reducing the effective bandwidth below the theoretical sum of the individual links. This overhead can be significant, especially with encrypted tunnels, where throughput can drop further. Second, the performance of the bonded tunnel may be limited by the device capabilities or license restrictions—for example, some devices or services (like SpeedFusion Connect) cap throughput at 200 Mbps, and enabling AES-256 encryption can halve the maximum bandwidth. Third, the quality and stability of the individual LTE links matter: packet loss, latency, or a single slow link can negatively affect the overall bonded performance. Fourth, configuration issues such as suboptimal outbound policy rules, bugs in policies involving domain names, or incorrect Latency Cutoff settings can prevent optimal traffic distribution and reduce observed speeds at the client. Lastly, differences in modem technology, antenna setup, or device limitations (such as on the Pepwave Max Transit Duo) may contribute, but user reports suggest that SpeedFusion itself is often the bottleneck, given that the same LTE links perform better on other hardware.

Peplink's new firmware version 8.1 introduces SpeedFusion Cloud, simplifying the bonding of multiple internet connections, such as cellular, USB tethered, and Ethernet, to enhance speed and reliability. Pepwave's SpeedFusion technology allows the simultaneous use of two connections, such as cellular and Wi-Fi, by sending a VPN over both connections and combining their speeds and reliability into a single virtual connection. query: What steps should a technician follow to set up a Pepwave MAX Transit Duo for combined, aggregated bandwidth using both AT&T and Verizon SIM cards to support reliable gaming and video conferencing, and what are the necessary licensing, configuration, and performance factors to consider?
answer: To achieve bonded, aggregated bandwidth from both AT&T and Verizon SIMs using a Pepwave MAX Transit Duo for high-availability tasks like gaming and video conferencing, the technician should install SIM cards from both carriers into the device’s dual modems. SpeedFusion bonding must be enabled, which is not automatic and requires a PrimeCare license (which includes 1TB of SpeedFusion Protect data for the first year) or the correct SKU, as well as activation via the device’s SFC Protect tab in the web UI. The technician can bond the two cellular connections either by connecting to SpeedFusion Cloud (which offers a free trial and then paid service) or by hosting a FusionHub Solo instance in the cloud (with a free license, but hosting costs). For the best results, both SIMs should be from different ISPs, and the SpeedFusion tunnel should be set up to aggregate bandwidth. Outbound policies should be configured to ensure both connections are used, avoiding session persistence, which would limit traffic to one WAN. WAN Smoothing and Forward Error Correction (FEC) should be disabled if the goal is to maximize throughput, as these features duplicate data and can reduce maximum speed. Performance will depend on device CPU and packet overhead, with real-world bonded throughput potentially lower than the sum of both links. Finally, the technician must consider increased data usage due to bonding and confirm that websites and streaming services function correctly over SpeedFusion VPN, as some may not.

## Document_2

When using SpeedFusion Cloud with a Peplink Balance One or Balance One Core, a SpeedFusion license is not required. However, if one intends to use SpeedFusion to connect to another Peplink device or FusionHub, then the SpeedFusion Bonding License Key would be necessary.

## Document_3

When using a Peplink Balance One or Balance One Core with SpeedFusion Cloud, the additional SpeedFusion Bonding License Key is not required. Users can purchase bandwidth top-up packs for SpeedFusion Cloud without needing the bonding license. Additionally, a care plan such as EssentialCare may include a package of 500GB/100Mbps for SpeedFusion Cloud, which can be beneficial for users looking to bond multiple DSL connections.

## Document_4

To direct specific machines to use specific WAN connections on the Peplink Balance 20/30 series, outbound policy can be utilized to control which server or type of traffic exits through which link. This ensures that return traffic comes back on the same link it was sent out on, maintaining the integrity of sessions such as FTP. If an FTP session is established on WAN1, Peplink will consistently route that FTP traffic through WAN1.

## Document_5

To disable drop-in mode on a Peplink 210 balancer device, navigate to Network > LAN > Drop-In Mode Settings. This may help resolve issues related to internet access after saving configurations, as drop-in mode can affect routing behavior.

## Document_6

The Balance One Core device does not support SpeedFusion Bandwidth Bonding without an optional license key (SKU: BPL-ONE-LC-SF). To bond two WAN connections, a SpeedFusion VPN tunnel must be established to a second Peplink device with SpeedFusion Bandwidth Bonding enabled or a FusionHub appliance. For instance, to bond two 30 Mbps WAN connections, a minimum WAN connection of 60 Mbps is required at the datacenter side.

The Peplink Balance 20 is suitable for small business use with up to 25 users, but the recommended user count is a guideline rather than a strict limit. ## Document_1

To configure VLANs on a Peplink Balance 20 router, it is important to set the port type correctly. For a specific VLAN, such as VLAN 4, the port should be set to 'Access' instead of 'Trunk'. This allows devices connected to that port to receive DHCP assignments from the designated VLAN. After changing the port settings, reconnecting the device should enable it to obtain the correct IP address from the VLAN's DHCP server.

## Document_2

To set up VLANs for voice and data on a Peplink device, navigate to Network > LAN > Network Settings and use the help icon to define multiple VLANs. Inter-VLAN routing is enabled by default, allowing communication between the defined VLANs. This setup will facilitate the use of both phones and PCs on the same port while ensuring proper routing through the Peplink device.

## Document_3

To set up a VLAN for a Meraki router on a Peplink Balance 20 without NAT, it is necessary to configure the VLAN settings appropriately. The Peplink Balance allows for full control over which VLANs can communicate on each LAN port, enabling the separation of networks for PCI compliance. Additionally, the use of unmanaged switches is possible with VLAN configuration on the router port, but the specifics of how they will function depend on the overall network setup and VLAN management.

## Document_4

The Peplink Balance 20X allows for the configuration of a Virtual WAN on LAN using Port-Based VLAN. Specifically, VLAN 5 can be set as the Virtual WAN, which reserves that VLAN. Additionally, LAN Port 2 can be configured as an 'Access Port' for VLAN 5, enabling a direct connection of an Internet modem or router to Port 2 as an access or untagged port.

## Document_5

To create a separate LAN for a neighbor using a Peplink Balance 20, VLANs should be configured. This involves setting up a second tagged VLAN on LAN Port 1 while ensuring that Inter-VLAN routing is turned off for both the existing LAN and the new VLAN. The switch must be configured to recognize VLAN 2 from the Ubiquiti AP and to send only VLAN 2 data packets out the Ethernet port connected to the Balance LAN Port 2. Additionally, the Balance router must be configured to expect VLAN tags on the data packets appropriately.

## Document_6

The Peplink Balance 380 does not support Port-Based VLAN settings, which are only available on models below the Balance 305. For detailed model comparisons, users can refer to the Peplink model comparison chart.

## Document_7

The PepLink Balance 310 supports Port Based VLANs and 802.1Q VLAN tagging, which can be configured for different LAN ports. To set up VLANs, the device should be in Bridged mode rather than Router mode, allowing the Balance to manage VLANs. Users can enable VLAN support in the Network settings and create applicable VLANs, then assign these VLANs to specified ports in the Port Settings.

## Document_8

All Peplink Balance models support port-based VLAN functionality, allowing for network segmentation and management based on specific ports.

## Document_9

To utilize port-based VLAN features on Peplink devices, firmware version 6.3 or above is required, with the current version being 7.1.2. The port type setting for configuring VLANs can be found under Network > LAN > Port Settings in the device's interface.

## Document_10

To route traffic between two subnets using a Peplink Balance 20, it is necessary to establish VLANs correctly. In this case, VLAN1 has been created on Port 4 with the subnet 192.168.1.x. For devices connected to this port, such as a laptop with a static IP of 192.168.1.250, to communicate with the gateway at 192.168.1.254, the LAN port 4 must be set to access mode on VLAN 1. By default, ports are set to trunk mode on untagged VLANs, which may prevent proper traffic flow.

## Document_11

To set up port-based VLAN on a Peplink Balance 20, it is important to ensure that the port type for port 4 is set to "Access". This configuration is necessary for the correct assignment of subnet IP via DHCP.

## Document_12

For proper VLAN configuration on a Peplink Balance 20 router, the LAN port must be set to Trunk mode to allow VLAN tags to be managed correctly. When using VLANs, the VLAN tag is attached to network packets by the Wireless Access Point (WAP), and the router processes these packets accordingly. It is also recommended to set up VLANs and SSIDs through InControl2 for better management.

## Document_13

To set up port-based VLANs on a Peplink Balance 20, configuration can be done under Network > LAN > Port Settings. Inter-VLAN routing is enabled by default, allowing clients from one VLAN to access devices on another VLAN without additional configuration.

## Document_14

To set up a Peplink Balance 20 for redundant network connectivity with 3 VLANs, it is necessary to configure port settings to map individual ports to specific LANs. However, issues may arise where client PCs lose network connectivity after this configuration. Inter-VLAN routing should be enabled to allow communication between different VLANs, such as a client from the 10.10.2.x network accessing another client on the 10.10.1.x network, but it may not function as expected without proper configuration.

## Document_15

To achieve traffic routing through a specific LAN port on a Pepwave Balance router, one can utilize port-based VLANs to create unique networks assigned to specific LAN ports. This setup can help facilitate access to external networks for devices like NAS and automation servers, even in a double NAT configuration.

## Document_16

To set up a Balance 20X for a cloud-based POS system with VLANs, it is necessary to manage the ports to avoid NAT conflicts. Disabling NAT for the Meraki router while retaining it for the office PCs is not feasible; instead, port forwarding can be configured for the Meraki system along with a static IP address outside the DHCP range. Two VLANs can be established, and the Balance 20X should be set to 'Access' mode for proper VLAN tagging, allowing unmanaged switches to function correctly without issues.

## Document_17

The Balance 20X supports Port-Based VLAN configuration, which can be used for Virtual WAN on LAN without needing an additional Layer 2 switch. However, the specifics regarding the number of Virtual WANs enabled by a single add-on license and the hardware throughput limits while using Virtual WAN on LAN4 are not detailed in the conversation.

## Document_18

To create a separate LAN for a neighbor using a Peplink Balance 20, one must create a VLAN and disable inter-VLAN routing for both the existing untagged LAN and the new tagged VLAN. This ensures that the two networks remain completely separated. The DHCP server that responds to a new device requesting an address is determined by the VLAN configuration and the device's connection to the network.

## Document_19

To create a separate LAN for a neighbor using a Peplink Balance 20, VLANs should be set up. A new SSID named 'NeighborNet' should be created and configured to use VLAN 2. Inter-VLAN routing should be turned off for both the existing LAN and the new VLAN to ensure complete separation. The DHCP server's response to a device's request for an address is determined by the VLAN configuration and the SSID the device connects to.

## Document_20

To create a separate LAN for a neighbor using a Peplink Balance 20, VLANs should be set up to ensure traffic isolation. It is important to turn off Inter-VLAN routing on both the existing LAN and the new tagged VLAN to maintain separation. The DHCP server that responds to a device's request for an address is determined by the VLAN configuration and tagging. Additionally, using a smart switch can help manage traffic, but it requires proper configuration to ensure that traffic is correctly isolated between the two LANs.

## Document_21

To create a separate LAN for a neighbor using a Peplink Balance 20, one should create a new VLAN (VLAN 2) with a different IP subnet and run a DHCP server for it on the Balance 20. This VLAN should be tied to LAN Port 2, which connects to a switch. To ensure isolation, the switch settings should limit the broadcast domain, preventing packets from VLAN 2 from being broadcast to other ports and vice versa. Specifically, set the PVID to 2 and enable ingress checking for the ports connected to VLAN 2 devices, ensuring that traffic is effectively isolated between the two VLANs.

## Document_22

The PepLink Balance 310 does not support multiple VLAN tagging on the WAN port and forwarding those tagged VLANs to the LAN side. For setups involving multiple VLANs, it is suggested to place the Balance 310 between a router, such as a D-link DIR-850-L, and a network switch to manage the connectivity effectively.

This opens a window prompting to define multiple VLANs; clicking 'here' switches the LAN settings to advanced mode with VLAN support. After confirming, apply the changes to enable VLAN functionality.

query: What steps are necessary to set up VLANs and port configurations on a Peplink Balance 20 to provide your neighbor with a completely segregated network, guaranteeing proper DHCP assignment and total isolation from your own network?
answer: To create a fully isolated network for a neighbor on a Peplink Balance 20, you should configure a new VLAN (e.g., VLAN 2) with its own IP subnet and enable a DHCP server for that VLAN. Assign this VLAN to a specific LAN port (such as LAN Port 2) and set the port type to 'Access' for VLAN 2, ensuring devices connected to this port receive IP addresses from the correct DHCP server. Turn off Inter-VLAN routing on both the existing LAN and the new VLAN to prevent communication between them, thereby guaranteeing complete traffic isolation. Additionally, configure the connected switch to recognize only VLAN 2 on the appropriate ports, using settings like PVID 2 and ingress checking, to maintain broadcast domain separation and prevent cross-VLAN traffic. Devices connected to the neighbor VLAN will only receive DHCP assignments and communicate within their isolated network.

## Document_4

To successfully stream HD video from a remote location using a CDN like Dcast, a MAX mobile router is required in the field along with an encoder solution. At the office or datacenter, a Peplink Balance 210 or higher should be used with a decoder solution. The quality of the stream is dependent on the bandwidth available from the carriers, and bonding multiple 3G connections can enhance the overall bandwidth.

## Document_5

Forming a Peplink Site-to-Site VPN between a Peplink Balance 210 and a MAX allows an encoder stream to utilize the combined bandwidth of all available 4G connections from the MAX, effectively streaming to a CDN through the 210's wired connection. The bonding efficiency is approximately 90%, meaning the maximum bonded throughput will be 90% of the total combined bandwidth, although actual performance may vary based on the real-time conditions of the underlying links. 4G connections are generally favorable for bonding in terms of bandwidth and latency.

## Document_6

When using the Max 700 router for video streaming applications, it is normal for a single video stream to utilize only one modem link at a time. To achieve true bonding and allow a single session to share bandwidth across multiple links, a Peplink Balance 210 or above can be used in a site-to-site VPN setup. The overall video performance will depend on the latency and speed of each internet connection being used.

## Document_7

A Peplink mobile router can establish secure VPN connections to a Peplink Balance router at a destination site, allowing for the bonding of multiple 3G connections to transport video streams. The bonding efficiency is approximately 90%, meaning that if each of the four 3G connections provides 512kbps, the total bonded bandwidth could reach around 1.8Mbps. The Peplink routers can compensate for varying connection speeds and latencies, intelligently routing traffic based on the real-time status of each connection, including effective bandwidth, latency, and packet loss.

## Document_8

The Pepwave MAX 700 can create IPsec tunnels to compatible devices such as Cisco, Juniper, or Peplink devices, allowing for one tunnel per WAN connection. It supports failover configurations to maintain IPsec connectivity if one WAN goes down. For enhanced bandwidth utilization, a Peplink Balance device (such as Balance 580 or above) can be used at the main office to create a Site-to-Site VPN with the MAX 700, utilizing VPN bonding technology to combine the bandwidth of all Internet links. The Pepwave MAX 700 has 2 Ethernet interfaces, supporting up to two DSL links, while the Peplink Balance 310 or above supports at least three Ethernet interfaces and one USB port for additional 3G/4G connectivity.

## Document_9

To achieve a reliable 1.5mbps bandwidth for real-time video streaming using bonded solutions, a Pepwave MAX device can be utilized in conjunction with a Pepwave Balance 380 or higher model for Site-to-Site VPN connections. This setup allows for aggregate throughput from multiple WANs, with approximately 90% of total bandwidth available after accounting for VPN overhead. The Peplink Site-to-Site VPN supports 256-bit AES encryption for secure data transmission. It is not necessary to use the same type of WAN connection on both ends of the tunnel, allowing flexibility in connection types. For handling 10 Site-to-Site VPN connections, the Balance 380 is recommended, which supports 20 connections and 60mb of bonded VPN throughput.

## Document_10

The MAX HD4 is capable of bonding multiple internet connections using SpeedFusion Bandwidth Bonding, which is a VPN technology. To achieve bandwidth bonding, a SpeedFusion VPN tunnel must be established to another Peplink SpeedFusion capable device or appliance, such as a Peplink Balance 305 or Peplink FusionHub located in a datacenter.

## Document_11

To achieve bonding of multiple SIM cards and a USB modem on a Pepwave MAX HD2 for streaming purposes, the SpeedFusion VPN Bandwidth Bonding functionality is required. The MAX HD2 supports this technology, allowing for the aggregation of WAN connections into a single high-throughput connection. The maximum throughput for SpeedFusion on the MAX HD2 is 100 Mbps without encryption and 60 Mbps with encryption. It is necessary to connect the MAX HD2 to a Peplink Balance 210, which should be located in a datacenter with a WAN connection speed that meets or exceeds the total bandwidth being bonded. Care should be taken to avoid including high latency connections in the bonding process, as they can negatively impact performance.

## Document_12

The Pepwave MAX 700 supports SpeedFusion VPN bonding technology, which allows for site-to-site VPN connections. To utilize this feature effectively, another SpeedFusion-enabled device is required on the opposite end, or alternatively, a FusionHub server can be deployed at a data center or in the cloud, such as on Amazon AWS.

## Document_13

To utilize SpeedFusion technology for secure corporate data uploads with a Pepwave MAX700, another SpeedFusion capable device is required at the headquarters. Alternatively, FusionHub, a software version of SpeedFusion, can be deployed on a virtual instance, including on Amazon's cloud.

## Document_14

Peplink's SpeedFusion technology is used for bandwidth aggregation and can work with VPNs. It does not require a centralized VPN or bandwidth terminal server. The MAX On-The-Go model supports bandwidth aggregation as well as load balancing. Compatibility with USB modems from Huawei and ZTE using CDMA technology is not explicitly confirmed in the response, but further details can be found on the provided links.

## Document_15

To achieve bonded internet connections using the Pepwave Max 700 with multiple USB modems, it is necessary to have two devices on either end of the internet connections to utilize Peplink's SpeedFusion technology, which allows for packet breakdown, transmission over different links, and reassembly. Without this setup, the Max 700 can still provide benefits through optimal configuration of outbound load balancing algorithms, but it will not achieve true bonding. Speed tests may not accurately reflect the combined speed of all connections, as they typically only utilize one connection for testing.

## Document_16

To achieve load balanced or bonded speeds for FTP/HTTP uploads using Pepwave MAX HD2 or MAX 700 routers with cellular modems, it is necessary to utilize SpeedFusion VPN bonding technology. This technology allows for the combination of multiple SIM cards to enhance upload speeds. A VPN Hub is required on the receiving end to reassemble the packets from the bonded connections, and the setup process is described as straightforward for users familiar with routers and IP configurations.

## Document_17

The Pepwave MAX Mobile router supports SpeedFusion VPN bonding, which allows for the aggregation of multiple WAN links such as 3G, 4G, and Wimax to connect to an enterprise network. With SpeedFusion bandwidth bonding, the combined bandwidth of two 3M connections can yield approximately 5.4M after accounting for system usage. To implement this solution, a Peplink Balance router is required at the headquarters or network operations center (NOC) to pair with the MAX Mobile router.

## Document_18

For remote internet solutions using bonded cellular connections, a Peplink Balance router is recommended over LTE routers. The user reports success with a setup using six LTE WANs bonded with SpeedFusion, achieving average speeds of 15-20 Mbps, which is the maximum throughput when encrypted through a VPN tunnel. However, the user acknowledges that there are various problems and limitations with this setup. Testing has shown that using multiple WAN connections does not consistently yield better speeds than a single connection, and issues such as dropped frames during video streaming with OBS were noted when using SpeedFusion.

## Document_19

Pepwave's SpeedFusion technology allows the simultaneous use of two connections, such as cellular and Wi-Fi, by sending a VPN over both connections and combining their speeds and reliability into a single virtual connection. This requires a server on the internet to handle the bonding, which can be hosted on platforms like Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure, utilizing Pepwave's free bonding server software license. The Max Transit Duo router, priced at $999, supports dual CAT 12 connections and is designed for users needing redundancy and uninterrupted connectivity, allowing both modems to be active simultaneously without manual switching. Testing is ongoing to explore configuration options for mobile users.

Peplink offers a range of products suitable for mobile applications, including devices with one to 18 active cellular modems that can bond connections, spread traffic, and create session persistence. The SpeedFusion VPN technology allows for bandwidth bonding with an overhead of approximately 20%, depending on the VPN type used. The new MBX model is 5G-ready and supports higher throughput capabilities compared to older models, making it suitable for demanding applications. Peplink products are available with various power supply options to accommodate different geographic regions.

The MAX HD4 can load balance across up to 4 cellular links, which is suitable for increasing bandwidth for multiple users. To aggregate and bond multiple SIM cards and a USB modem for a single high-capacity connection using a Pepwave Max HD2, SpeedFusion Bonding technology is required. This involves using two SpeedFusion VPN appliances, with one being a FusionHub Appliance hosted in the cloud. This setup allows for continuous connectivity necessary for streaming applications like Wirecast to Facebook Live. To aggregate and bond multiple SIM cards and a USB modem for a stable connection suitable for streaming with Wirecast, it is essential to have a stable public-facing IP address on SpeedFusion, which can be achieved using a physical Balance router or a virtual appliance like FusionHub. A MAX router may also be suitable depending on the licensing and connection requirements. This setup is necessary to ensure a continuous connection for streaming purposes.

To aggregate and bond multiple SIM cards and a USB modem for a single connection on a Max HD 2, utilizing Peplink's SpeedFusion technology is necessary. This setup allows for the creation of a 'thick pipe' for continuous streaming, which is essential for applications like Facebook Live. Users may need to seek assistance from Peplink partners for deploying FusionHub, as advanced networking knowledge is required for proper configuration.

When using a Pepwave Max 700 with multiple USB modems for bonded internet, the maximum speed achieved may be limited by the shared bandwidth of the cellular connections, especially if they are from the same carrier. To optimize the speed of an aggregated connection using the Pepwave Max 700 with multiple USB modems, it is suggested to utilize the Bandwidth Management feature to reserve or cap bandwidth for individual clients based on their IP addresses. query: What is the recommended configuration process for a technician setting up a Pepwave MAX 700 or MAX HD2 to enable bonded video streaming from a remote location, and what critical elements influence the system's performance and throughput in this scenario?
answer:
To configure a Pepwave MAX 700 or MAX HD2 for bonded video streaming from a remote site, the technician should utilize SpeedFusion VPN bonding technology. This requires setting up a SpeedFusion VPN tunnel from the MAX device to another SpeedFusion-capable device, such as a Peplink Balance 210 or higher at the receiving site, or to a FusionHub virtual appliance hosted in a data center or cloud environment (e.g., AWS). This setup allows aggregation and bonding of multiple SIM cards and USB modems into a single high-throughput connection, which is essential for continuous and reliable video streaming.

Key factors affecting performance and throughput include:
- The total available bandwidth of the aggregated WAN connections, and the efficiency of SpeedFusion bonding (typically about 90% of the combined bandwidth due to VPN overhead).
- The real-time latency and variability of each WAN link; including high-latency links can negatively affect overall performance.
- The throughput limitations of the MAX device itself (e.g., MAX HD2 supports up to 100 Mbps unencrypted/60 Mbps encrypted SpeedFusion throughput).
- The capabilities and throughput rating of the receiving device (e.g., Balance 210, 380, or FusionHub) must meet or exceed the total bonded bandwidth.
- The type and quality of the cellular connections; using different carriers can help avoid bandwidth sharing limitations.
- Proper bandwidth management on the MAX 700 can help reserve or cap bandwidth for video clients to optimize performance.
- Testing with speed tests may not accurately reflect true bonded speeds, as most tests use only a single connection.

In summary, effective bonded video streaming requires the correct pairing of SpeedFusion-enabled devices, careful selection and configuration of WAN links, and attention to both device and link throughput limitations.

## Document_1

When using Peplink Balance routers with Content Filtering enabled, blocking the Security/Tunneling protocol of IPSec can interfere with Wi-Fi Calling functionality, as Wi-Fi Calling requires this protocol. The Exempted Domain feature in Web Blocking does not exempt IPSec application blocking, which may lead to issues with Wi-Fi Calling. Users experiencing this problem are advised to open a support ticket for further assistance and investigation into the conditions under which the Wi-Fi Calling application is blocked.

## Document_2

If one Balance 30 router successfully upgraded to firmware version 8.1 while the other remains on version 5.3.12, it is possible that the router stuck on 5.3.12 was too outdated to perform a direct upgrade to 8.1.0. It is also recommended to check if both routers are the exact same hardware revision, as differences in hardware could affect firmware compatibility and upgrade paths.

## Document_3

To successfully upgrade a Peplink Balance 30 router from firmware version 5.3.12 to 8.1, it may be necessary to first upgrade to an intermediate version, such as 7, before proceeding to version 8. This can be done by accessing the archived firmware versions in the router's firmware management section.

## Document_4

The Peplink Balance 700, released in 2006, is considered outdated and should be replaced for security reasons. If one chooses to keep it, the minimum recommended firmware version is 6.3.4, which requires upgrading through several intermediate versions: 5.0, 5.3.12, and 5.4.9 before reaching 6.1.0 and finally 6.3.4. The firmware for version 5 is not publicly available and requires logging a support ticket to obtain.

## Document_5

To upgrade a Peplink Balance 30 LTE from firmware version 6.1.2 to 7.1.2, users should ensure that the firmware upload is successful. If the online upgrade method fails, the manual upgrade method can be attempted by directing the device to the correct .bin file for the firmware version. Users should verify that the firmware image is compatible and that the upload process is functioning correctly, as issues may arise if the upload does not progress or if the device remains on the previous firmware version after the attempt.

## Document_6

To upgrade a Balance 30 LTE (model BPL031-LTE-A-T) from firmware version 6.1.2 to 7.1.2, it is recommended to reboot the device before attempting the manual upgrade again. Connecting a laptop directly to the LAN port of the Balance 30 LTE may facilitate the upgrade process.

## Document_8

To upgrade a Peplink Balance 30 from firmware version 5.3.12 build 1303 to the latest firmware 7.1.0, it is necessary to first upgrade to firmware release 5.4.9 to avoid potential issues during the upgrade process.

To resolve a firmware upgrade failure on a Peplink Balance 20 Hardware revision 6 running firmware 6.3.1 build 3138, it is recommended to reboot the device before attempting the upgrade again.

The device has attempted the upgrade multiple times but has reverted to its previous firmware version with a log note indicating a failure.

## Document_12

The Peplink Balance 2500-2SFP supports dual rate SFP+ modules, which can operate at 1 Gbps speed. A list of compatible SFP modules that have been tested with this device is available for reference.

## Document_13

To update a Peplink Balance 220 from an outdated firmware version, it is recommended to follow a stepwise upgrade path: first to version 5.4.9, then to 6.3.3, and finally to 7.0.0. The firmware archives can be accessed on the Peplink site, and a firmware unlock key is required to upgrade to version 6.3.3.

## Document_14

The current firmware version for the Peplink Balance 30 is 6.3.3, with an option to jump directly to version 7.0 if the router is only managing multiple WAN links without additional features like AP controller, VPN tunnels, or VLANs. It is recommended to download the firmware to a computer and perform a manual upload, ensuring to back up the current configuration before proceeding. Caution is advised when skipping multiple firmware versions, and seeking assistance from Peplink support is suggested for more reliable guidance.

To upgrade the firmware on a Balance 30 LTE that is experiencing issues, it is recommended to first update to firmware version 6.1.1 (build 2530) using the provided link, allowing up to 30 minutes for the process. After successfully updating to 6.1.1, the next step is to upgrade to firmware version 6.3.3 (build 3231) using another provided link.

## Document_16

To upgrade the firmware on a Peplink Balance 700 from version 4, the device must first be updated to version 4.8.2, then to 5.3.12, and finally to the highest version 5.4.9. Users are advised to open a support ticket for specific links and instructions regarding the firmware upgrade process.

## Document_17

The latest firmware build for the Balance 30 is 5.4.10, which can be downloaded from the provided link. To upgrade to 6.x firmware, the unit must be brought back under warranty, as indicated in the upgrade guide.

## Document_18

To upgrade a Peplink Balance 30 from firmware version 4.8.1 build 1106 to the latest firmware version 6.x, the upgrade must be performed in a specific sequence. First, upgrade to firmware version 5.2.2, then to 5.4.10 build 1769, and finally to 6.1.2 build 2717.

## Document_19

To upgrade from firmware version 4.8 to 5.4 on a Peplink device, it is advisable to refer to the Peplink knowledge base for specific instructions regarding the upgrade process. This includes checking for any necessary updates or unlock keys that may be required during the upgrade to ensure a smooth transition with minimal downtime.

## Document_20

To enable Wi-Fi Calling while blocking the IPSec tunneling protocol using Peplink Balance routers, it is necessary to utilize a new option for "Exempted Domains from Application Blocking" in the content filtering settings. Issues have been noted with firmware versions 7.1.2GA and 8.0.0RC4, and further testing is being conducted with firmware 8.0.1 RC4 to find a solution for maintaining Wi-Fi Calling functionality while restricting VPN traffic.

## Document_21

The SFP ports on the Peplink Balance 2500-2SFP are capable of supporting a 1 G SFP, allowing for 1Gbps speed operation.

## Document_22

The Peplink Balance 2500-2SFP supports 1 Gbps SFP modules, allowing it to connect to a 1 Gbps switch without issues.

## Document_24

query: How do the Max Transit Duo (featuring dual CAT-12 modems), Max Transit CAT-18, and Max Transit 5G models differ in their performance for mobile use cases that need concurrent Wi-Fi as WAN and cellular connectivity, and what are the main restrictions and factors to keep in mind for each of these models?
answer:
The Max Transit Duo (dual CAT-12) is the recommended model for mobile applications that require simultaneous use of Wi-Fi as WAN and cellular connections because it supports bonding and outbound policies for this configuration. In contrast, the Max Transit CAT-18 cannot use Wi-Fi as WAN and cellular at the same time due to lack of outbound policy support, despite its higher modem category and increased sensitivity (which is beneficial in rural areas). The Max Transit 5G, featuring a Cat 20 modem, is designed for future-proofing with higher speeds, but its CPU limits real-world throughput to 400 Mbps, and the device may not fully utilize 5G capabilities at this time.

Key considerations include:
- The Max Transit Duo supports SpeedFusion bonding for improved reliability and performance but has a maximum throughput of 400 Mbps and may require licensing (PrimeCare, SpeedFusion) for advanced features like WAN smoothing.
- The Max Transit CAT-18 offers better sensitivity and supports multiple SIMs but cannot bond Wi-Fi as WAN with cellular, limiting its flexibility in certain mobile scenarios.
- The Max Transit 5G provides higher theoretical speeds with a Cat 20 modem but is CPU-limited and may not be certified on all carriers yet, making it less practical for immediate deployment where simultaneous Wi-Fi as WAN and cellular use is required.
- All models may require additional access points or external antennas to ensure adequate Wi-Fi coverage inside and outside vehicles, especially in environments with signal-impeding materials like stainless steel.
- Users should also consider the compatibility of cellular data plans and potential carrier restrictions on modem use.

Overall, for mobile scenarios needing bonded Wi-Fi as WAN and cellular, the Max Transit Duo (dual CAT-12) is the preferred and most flexible solution currently available.

The Pepwave MAX Transit CAT 18 has two USB power input ports, each rated at 5V and 2A, which together provide a total of 10W. To address WAN DNS faults from the VSAT input on WAN 1, it is suggested to change the health check method to ping, targeting either the terminal or an internet address such as google.com. DNS lookups on VSAT can fail due to higher latency, and in many cases, it is recommended to disable the health check on VSAT entirely, as it is typically used only as a last resort.

The SKU for the Mounting Bracket for the AP One Enterprise is ACW-779. To order a replacement mount, it is recommended to contact a certified Value-Added Distributor (VAD) for assistance.

## Document_4

The Pepwave MAX Transit Duo requires a high current supply of 2.4 Amps to operate properly on USB power. If using multiple lower current supplies, it is important to utilize both USB connectors to meet the necessary power requirements.

## Document_5

The Pepwave Transit Duo can be powered using a Micro USB supplying 5V at 2A or through a DC input ranging from 12 to 48V DC at 2A, which can be connected via the terminal block or barrel socket.

## Document_6

When configuring port numbers for secure web administration on the SOHO MK3, it is advisable to avoid common ports to prevent conflicts with services that may already be using them. Choosing port numbers above 1023 is generally considered safe, as ports from 0 to 1023 are well-known ports assigned to common protocols, while ports from 1024 to 49151 are registered ports assigned to specific services. The dynamic port range from 49152 to 65535 can be used by any service on an ad hoc basis, as they are assigned when a session is established and released when the session ends.

Replacement terminal block plugs are available for purchase from 5Gstore, which keeps them in stock.

The BR1 mini (HW3) is being launched as a replacement for the discontinued BR1 MK2. ## Document_13

For repair and replacement parts for broken antennas on a Pepwave device, it is recommended to log a ticket with engineering for assistance with RMA and repair services.

Replacement rack mount kits for the Pepwave MAX HD4, known as Ear Mounts, can be ordered from any Peplink partner using the product code ACW-731. These rack mount kits are also compatible with the Peplink Balance 210 and 310 models.

To create more than two IPSEC VPN links from a PepWave Max700 device, an additional PepVPN license is required. This license can be purchased from a Peplink Partner or through the Peplink Store.

## Document_16

To confirm the compatibility of the Pepwave SURF SOHO MK3 with replacement units, it is advisable to contact the seller directly to ensure the correct model is being purchased. The official specifications can be referenced at the Peplink website to verify the product details.

The Pepwave MAX Transit Duo may not operate correctly on 5V USB power if the USB cable is faulty or if the device requires more power due to the installation of two SIM cards and the creation of a tunnel. Insufficient voltage can cause the battery light to flash red every 10 seconds, indicating a power issue.

Peplink periodically refreshes its hardware and discontinues certain models in favor of newer ones, although there are no known issues with the discontinued model mentioned. While the distributor no longer notifies partners of discontinuations, replacements may still be available from existing stock. The firmware across models remains similar, minimizing the learning curve for users transitioning to newer models.

The BR1 MK2 has been discontinued due to severe supply chain issues affecting its main System on Chip (SoC), which is linked to the global semiconductor chip shortage. A replacement product, the BR1 mini (HW3), is being launched and is expected to have a smooth transition for users migrating from the BR1 MK2, with most certifications either completed or in progress.

query: What steps should a technician take to guarantee dependable USB power for the Pepwave MAX Transit Duo and MAX Transit CAT 18, particularly during heavy usage or when dual SIM cards or tunnels are active?
answer: For the Pepwave MAX Transit Duo, reliable operation on USB power requires a high current supply of 2.4A. If only lower current USB supplies are available, both USB connectors must be used to meet the device’s power needs. If the device is under high load (e.g., using two SIM cards and creating a tunnel), insufficient voltage or a faulty USB cable may cause power issues, such as the battery light flashing red every 10 seconds. The MAX Transit CAT 18 has two USB power input ports, each rated at 5V 2A (totaling 10W), but its power consumption is 18W, so both ports must be powered simultaneously with separate sources to provide adequate power and enable battery cycling without downtime. Failing to meet these requirements can result in unreliable operation or the device failing to power up properly.

To direct specific machines to use specific WAN connections on the Peplink Balance 20/30 series, outbound policy can be utilized to control which server or type of traffic exits through which link. This ensures that return traffic comes back on the same link it was sent out on, maintaining the integrity of sessions such as FTP. If an FTP session is established on WAN1, Peplink will consistently route that FTP traffic through WAN1.

In contrast, the Peplink Balance 20X has been noted to handle multiple WAN connections effectively without speed reduction, even when using VLANs.

Additionally, static routes may need to connect to gateways within the same subnet, which can complicate configurations if sites are not willing to share a common subnet.

This indicates that proper routing and policy settings are essential for enabling connectivity between satellite sites and Azure.

## Document_2

For high availability (HA) configurations with Peplink Balance 710 devices, using an active/active setup is recommended over an active/passive VRRP HA-pair due to the slow failover times associated with VRRP, which can exceed 30 seconds. In cases where compliance requires an active/passive configuration, VRRP may still be used, but it is considered cumbersome and outdated compared to active/active configurations that allow for faster failover and better resource utilization.

## Document_3

In a high availability (HA) setup using Peplink Balance routers in NAT mode, VRRP is utilized for WAN as well as LAN configurations. When properly configured, VRRP allows for the transfer of WAN addresses from the master router to the slave router in the event of a failure. This means that only one public IP address is needed for the HA setup, as the slave router will take over the master router's public IP address upon failure, rather than requiring multiple public IP addresses for each router.

## Document_4

In a high availability (HA) setup for Peplink Balance routers in NAT mode, the LAN configuration requires a Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) setup with a virtual IP (VIP) for the master and slave units. For the WAN configuration, two options are presented. Option 1 requires three VRRP groups: one for the LAN and one for each ISP, necessitating a total of six public IP addresses. Option 2 suggests a simpler configuration with only two public IP addresses, where the master unit handles both WAN connections and the slave unit takes over the WAN IP address upon failover. The WAN setup involves two ISPs, each with its own subnet and gateway.

## Document_5

In a High Availability (HA) setup using two Peplink Balance 380 routers configured with VRRP, issues may arise when both routers compete for the master role, particularly during internet connectivity loss. This can lead to network downtime as the routers transition between master and slave roles. The VRRP protocol relies on periodic advertisement packets sent from the master device to maintain the master-slave relationship. If both routers remain connected to the LAN and are aware of each other's WAN connectivity, conflicts over the master role can occur, especially if one router fails to recognize the recovery of the other after a power cycle. Proper diagnostics and physical connection details are crucial for troubleshooting these issues effectively.

## Document_6

Pepwave routers support high availability configurations using the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) as defined in RFC 3768, allowing for redundancy and failover in a master-slave arrangement. In this configuration, two Pepwave routers communicate over the LAN using VRRP, broadcasting heartbeat signals at a frequency of one per second. If the master router fails to send a heartbeat signal for 3 seconds or longer, the slave router activates, initiates WAN connections, and binds to a preconfigured LAN IP address. Upon recovery, the master router will regain its active status by default.

## Document_7

Peplink Balance devices, specifically the Balance 210 or above and MAX 700/HD, support High Availability (HA) failover using Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP). In an HA setup, the master device sends periodic VRRP advertisement packets to specific multicast addresses, allowing the slave device to take over if the master fails. The configuration requires both devices to be on the same subnet and use the same HA group identifier. The virtual IP (VIP) serves as the default gateway for all LAN hosts. Configuration Sync can be enabled for the slave unit to automatically apply changes from the master unit. The failover process typically takes 10-15 seconds, and both devices must be connected to the internet in the same mode, either NAT or Drop-in mode.

In some cases, such as with Balance 710 and VRRP, failover times can exceed 30 seconds due to protocol limitations, making active/active HA preferable for faster recovery.

## Document_2

When changing the handshake port on a Pepwave MAX hotspot, the new port should take effect immediately after the changes are applied. If the device continues to use the original port for handshaking, it is recommended to open a support ticket for further assistance.

## Document_3

In a Pepwave Transit Pro (Duo) setup with 4 active SIMs and Fusion Connect Active, SpeedFusion Connect functions as an additional connection option, effectively acting like a third SIM slot for each modem. Users can select between connecting to the primary SIMs (A/B) or the SpeedFusion Connect (SFConnect).

## Document_4

The modem firmware updater for the Pepwave Transit CAT18 device will be fully functional in the upcoming 8.1.0 device firmware release. The user is confirmed to be on the latest modem firmware version, which is 32.00.124 for the Telit LM960 model.

## Document_5

The Pepwave Transit models with Cat 12 modems support download speeds of up to 600 Mbps, while those with Cat 6 modems support speeds of up to 300 Mbps. The newest 'Pro' versions of the Pepwave Transit are equipped with Cat 12 modems.

## Document_6

The MAX BR1 MK2 may face connectivity issues with T-Mobile if it does not support the bands that T-Mobile uses in certain areas, specifically bands 7 and 12. The router is currently connecting to Band 5, which may not be sufficient for optimal performance. To check the primary band being used by an iPhone, one can enter the code ***3001#12345#*** to access the serving cell information.

## Document_7

The issue of GPS location updates failing on Pepwave devices may be related to the GPS antenna rather than the devices themselves. Users have reported intermittent functionality with both a 7 in 1 antenna and the GPS antenna provided with the Transit DUO and Transit Pro. The GPS signal may resume after rebooting the router, suggesting potential reliability issues with the antennas. For persistent problems, it is recommended to download a diagnostic file from the status page and submit a ticket to Peplink engineering for further investigation.

## Document_8

To improve connectivity issues with a Pepwave Transit Duo, it is advised to use a dedicated wireless access point (AP) instead of using WiFi WAN and an AP simultaneously, as this can lead to disconnections when there are issues with the WiFi WAN.

## Document_9
