The 210 acts as a DHCP server for its LAN and should allow devices on the 198.42.231.0 network to communicate with devices on the 198.42.232.0 network if properly configured.

The USSD feature on the Pepwave Max BR1 was broken in firmware version 6.3.3 build 2252, as USSD codes enclosed in hashtags (like #123#) return an 'invalid USSD code' error, while they function correctly in firmware version 6.3.1 build 2023. Users are advised to revert to version 6.3.1 for proper functionality until the issue is resolved. There is no confirmation regarding the functionality of hashtag symbols in USSD codes with version 7 firmware, and users should be cautious about upgrading without this information.

A beta build of the MAX BR1 firmware is available for testing, which can be found in the Eval Guide on the Peplink forum. The fully tested and current firmware can be downloaded from the Peplink support website.
WPA3 security policy is only available in the SOHO MK3 model of the Pepwave Surf Soho series. Users with hardware revision 2 will not have access to this feature in firmware version 8.1.1.
The latest factory firmware for the Surf200 SPW-212 can be downloaded from the Peplink support downloads page at http://www.peplink.com/support/downloads/.
The latest factory firmware for the Surf200 SPW-212 can be downloaded from the direct link provided: http://download.pepwave.com/surfap/fw_090050.bin.

The upcoming 6.3 GA firmware for FusionHub will not include support for Static Route and Layer 2 features. However, a version of the firmware that supports static routes is available for download through a provided link.

To troubleshoot connectivity issues with the Peplink Balance 20X when using cable internet, it is suggested to consider the network setup, particularly whether the ISP provides a router. In such cases, the ISP's router should be treated as the first router, with the Peplink acting as the second router. This configuration can enhance security by preventing the ISP from accessing detailed network information. The Peplink Balance 20X offers a good level of security out of the box, and additional security layers can be implemented through VLANs and access rules, depending on the complexity of the network environment.

The Balance 20X may experience connectivity issues with certain cable modems, which is a known problem that has not yet been resolved. For initial setup and security configuration, instructions for the Surf SOHO can also be applied to the Balance 20X, as the user interface is mostly similar. Additionally, using a Peplink product is generally more secure than using a standard ISP router or devices like Synology NAS, which prioritize sharing over security.

The Balance 20X may experience connectivity issues with cable internet, potentially due to problems with the ISP, as indicated by packet capture analysis. In a similar case, a user faced connection issues with a Protectli FW4B and resolved the problem by introducing an Asus router between the devices, suggesting that using an additional router may help in troubleshooting connectivity problems with cable modems.

There is a known bug related to connectivity issues with the Peplink Balance 20X that has been previously documented in a forum thread. Troubleshooting efforts may be necessary to resolve the connectivity problems, particularly when using cable internet with Comcast. The specific details of the bug and potential solutions can be found in the referenced thread.

To resolve connectivity issues with the Peplink Balance 20X, it is recommended to follow a specific power cycling protocol: unplug all devices including the modem and router for 20 minutes, then plug in the Balance 20X first and allow it to sit for five minutes before connecting the modem and Cat cable. After this procedure, the device should establish a stable connection. The user reported successful connectivity after applying firmware version 8.1.3 and noted that the connection remained stable for two days without interruption, except when intentionally disconnected.

To access the WDS option in the AP tab, users may need to download firmware version 3.5.4 from the Peplink support downloads archive, ensuring that the firmware matches the hardware revision of their access point.

In firmware version 3.6 of Pepwave AP products, the WDS (Wireless Distribution System) option has been eliminated from the web interface, which has caused issues for users relying on this feature for connectivity in situations without Ethernet cabling. Users have expressed concerns about the lack of communication regarding this change, as the documentation still references the WDS feature, and they advocate for better transparency in release notes regarding feature changes in future firmware updates.

The firmware version 3.6 does not include the WDS option in the AP tab, as noted in the release notes for that specific version. Users should be aware of this limitation when skipping firmware versions during updates.

To resolve issues with downloading AP firmware pack 1171 from a Balance One Core dashboard, it is suggested to delete any older firmware versions before attempting to download the latest one again. This may help in overcoming the spinning progress indicator issue.

To ensure the correct firmware is downloaded for the Peplink Balance 210 HW4, it is recommended to use the device's firmware upgrade feature located under System > Firmware > Check for Firmware. Additionally, InControl2 can be utilized to manage firmware policy effectively.

There is a confirmed bug in the 7.1 firmware on the Balance One Core that affects the sorting functionality of the Download and Upload columns in the 'Status: Client list' for online clients. This issue has been acknowledged and is targeted to be fixed in an upcoming firmware release.
query: What detailed troubleshooting steps, including firmware checks and network configuration actions, should a technician take to address ongoing connectivity problems between a Balance 20X device and a cable modem?
answer: A technician should first ensure the Balance 20X is running the latest firmware, as a bug related to connectivity was fixed in version 8.1.1. If issues persist, upgrade to 8.1.3, as users have reported stable connections after applying this version. Next, the technician should power cycle both the modem and router by unplugging all devices for 20 minutes, then plugging in the Balance 20X first and waiting five minutes before reconnecting the modem and Ethernet cable. If connection problems still occur, consider the network topology: if the ISP provides a router, set up the Balance 20X as a secondary router behind the ISP's router to improve compatibility and security. If the modem is still not compatible, introducing an intermediate router between the modem and the Balance 20X may help resolve persistent issues. Throughout this process, refer to community forums and documentation for known bugs and additional troubleshooting steps.

## Document_1

For a work from home setup requiring reliable internet for VoIP and video calls, a Peplink Balance30LTE with SpeedFusion Cloud is recommended, as it provides stable connectivity even with multiple users streaming content. The user has successfully transitioned to using only Starlink and a local WISP, eliminating the need for LTE, and reports better stability compared to traditional ISPs. Future-proofing considerations include the potential for Starlink to achieve download speeds exceeding 200 Mbps, suggesting that specifications should be reviewed before purchasing a router.

## Document_2

When testing the SpeedFusion speed over a Starlink WAN with a Balance 210 Generation 4, speeds can vary significantly based on the configuration. Direct connections to the Starlink Ethernet adapter can yield speeds up to 120 Mbps, while routing through the Balance 210 shows reduced speeds of around 80 Mbps. Factors affecting performance may include the use of encryption, the specific model of Starlink, MTU settings, and the condition of Ethernet adapters or modems. Testing from a local device and using tools like Lan Speed Test can help rule out other issues.

## Document_3

When using SpeedFusion with a Starlink connection, users may experience lower speeds compared to direct testing of the Starlink service. In this case, a user reported achieving only about 41% of the Starlink speed when routed through SpeedFusion, with speeds around 65 Mbps compared to direct tests showing 150+ Mbps. Additionally, packet loss and out-of-order packets may negatively impact SpeedFusion performance over Starlink, suggesting that network conditions can affect the efficiency of the connection.

## Document_4

SpeedFusion VPN is a suitable solution for aggregating multiple internet connections to enhance stability and reduce disconnects. It includes features such as Hot Failover, which automatically switches to another available connection during a failure, ensuring no downtime. WAN Smoothing addresses packet loss by sending extra packets that can be reconstructed, while also optimizing traffic to the connection with the lowest latency. Bandwidth Bonding combines multiple connections into a single high-speed connection, though it may not be necessary for all setups. It is important to note that SpeedFusion VPN requires Peplink devices on both ends of the tunnel for operation.

## Document_5

Using a SpeedFusion tunnel with a combination of Starlink RV and cellular connections, a performance of approximately 180 Mbps was achieved. The setup was tested in a major metro area, specifically on top of a parking garage during mid-day, indicating good performance under those conditions. Further testing of Starlink alone through the tunnel is planned for additional performance insights.

## Document_6

SpeedFusion has been tested with Starlink and functions similarly to any other WAN connection. It can be used for bonding due to the lower latency compared to traditional satellite connectivity.

## Document_7

SpeedFusion bonding over Starlink has been reported to work perfectly in the UK countryside. Additionally, the user plans to improve their LTE experience by deploying external antennas.

## Document_8

SpeedFusion (SF) works fine over Starlink, but there is a limitation in accessing the management interface at 192.168.100.1, which requires workarounds until Peplink provides static routes on the WAN interfaces. Future developments may include mobile terminals for Starlink that can be used in RVs, but these will likely be more expensive and different from standard consumer kits, similar to the distinction between marine VSAT antennas and residential satellite dishes.

## Document_9

SpeedFusion and PepVPN can achieve download speeds of up to 150 Mbps and upload speeds of 30 Mbps over Starlink, with reliable performance typically in the 100 Mbps range. However, users may experience intermittent outages lasting around 20 seconds, which can be tuned with health checks. Statistics indicate periods of no satellite connection and other outages, suggesting that while the connection is suitable for streaming and downloading, an additional WAN connection is recommended for full stability, especially for critical applications requiring a SpeedFusion tunnel.

## Document_10

SpeedFusion and PepVPN performance over Starlink experiences intermittent outages, which are categorized by Starlink as 'obstructed' (loss of signal with a satellite in sight), 'No Sat' (signal loss with no satellites in the correct geometry), and 'Beta downtime' (general ping loss). The outages occur approximately every 45 minutes and last for 5-10 seconds, with the majority being classified as Beta downtime (about 75%) and the rest as No Sat (about 25%). The maximum recorded downtime has been 4 minutes per day, with WAN connection logs indicating frequent disconnections due to HTTP test failures.

## Document_11

Users are experiencing varying performance with SpeedFusion and PepVPN over Starlink. One user reported achieving 80-100 Mbps when connected directly to Starlink or through a Pepwave MAX Transit without PepVPN, but noted a significant drop to about 12 Mbps when using SpeedFusion with a Balance 210 router. In contrast, the same Balance 210 achieved over 20 Mbps with Verizon as the WAN. Previously, the same setup had performed at 80 Mbps with SpeedFusion at a different location before switching to Starlink. Troubleshooting is needed to determine the cause of the performance issues with SpeedFusion over Starlink.

## Document_12

After upgrading the firmware of FusionHub and Balance from version 4.1.3 to 4.2.0, and changing the Forward Error Correction (FEC) setting from off to LOW, the performance of SpeedFusion over Starlink was tested. With one WAN connected (Balance 210 via Ethernet and Max Transit CAT 18 using Wi-Fi as WAN on 5GHz), the download speed achieved was 61 Mbps to Cloudflare over SpeedFusion, compared to 108 Mbps without SpeedFusion. This is an improvement over previous speeds of 12 Mbps on Starlink, although it is lower than the 80 to 89 Mbps experienced on a 100 Mbps DSL WAN at a different location.

## Document_13

When using SpeedFusion over Starlink, performance can vary significantly based on the speed test site and connection quality. Optimal settings included bonding as the method, with Forward Error Correction (FEC) turned off, using Verizon for upload only and Starlink for download only. The best recorded speeds were 66.40 Mbps for download and 44.01 Mbps for upload, although results varied widely depending on the test server used. WAN Quality analysis indicated speeds of 110-150 Mbps on the WAN side, suggesting potential for higher performance under different conditions.

## Document_14

SpeedFusion can effectively manage connections by allowing users to bond multiple WAN sources, such as a WISP connection and Starlink, to ensure seamless internet access. In scenarios where Starlink experiences outages, SpeedFusion can automatically switch to the WISP connection, maintaining service continuity for applications like Zoom meetings, even when Starlink drops multiple times.

## Document_15

For users experiencing frequent signal drops with Starlink as a WAN connection, it is noted that the Starlink service can drop out for a few seconds multiple times a day, which may lead to 'no cable detected' messages on devices like the Balance 30 LTE. To mitigate these issues, using SpeedFusion Cloud to bond Starlink with a secondary fixed wireless ISP connection can effectively maintain a stable connection, preventing interruptions during calls on platforms like Teams or Zoom. This setup allows for seamless connectivity even during short outages, with minimal data usage reported.

## Document_16

Peplink's SpeedFusion technology allows for efficient bandwidth management by creating sub-tunnels for different applications, enabling hot failover between various WAN connections such as fiber, broadband, and bonded 5G or Starlink. Each sub-tunnel can be configured with specific outbound policies tailored to the needs of applications like Microsoft Teams or Zoom, ensuring smooth performance even under varying network conditions. The technology incorporates features like WAN smoothing and forward error correction (FEC) to enhance reliability and throughput, particularly in scenarios with packet loss, such as with Starlink connections. Peplink provides tools like the WAN Analyzer to assess non-bonded throughput and optimize performance by accounting for bonding overhead. A forthcoming SpeedFusion white paper will detail these technologies and their advantages over competitors, serving as a resource for Peplink partners and users.

## Document_17

Peplink's SpeedFusion technology enables bandwidth bonding by combining multiple WAN connections, such as fixed and cellular links, to enhance throughput and reliability. This technology allows for the creation of a robust internet connection by bonding different types of networks, including Starlink and cellular, which compensates for dropouts and optimizes data traffic through dynamic weighted bonding. Additionally, SpeedFusion includes WAN smoothing, which sends copies of data packets across multiple WAN links to ensure a jitter-free data stream, and hot failover, which maintains session continuity during link failures. Peplink's solutions can be configured as standalone SD-WAN devices or integrated into existing SD-WAN setups. The InControl2 platform provides management capabilities for Peplink devices, enabling configuration, monitoring, and reporting, while also supporting geographic functionalities and remote management through mobile applications.

The discussion revolves around the use of Peplink's SpeedFusion technology for optimizing internet connectivity, particularly in scenarios where multiple connections, such as a cable modem and Starlink, are utilized. The setup allows for seamless failover, ensuring that critical applications like Zoom and Teams calls remain active during outages. The latest firmware (8.3) introduces SFC Protect, which enhances the capabilities of SpeedFusion, while previous versions (8.2.1) still support similar features like WAN smoothing. The importance of assessing connection quality during failover situations is emphasized, as both connections may not always provide adequate performance. The conversation also touches on the necessity of having multiple reliable links to ensure consistent connectivity and the benefits of directly connecting devices to the Peplink router instead of using intermediary routers. Overall, the effectiveness of SpeedFusion in managing bandwidth, mitigating packet loss, and improving connection stability is highlighted.

## Document_19

Peplink provides solutions for enhancing mobile connectivity in challenging environments, such as remote locations with poor signal. The use of SpeedFusion technology allows for the bonding of multiple connections, including Starlink and cellular links, to ensure reliable internet access. Key features include WAN smoothing, which duplicates traffic to minimize packet loss and latency during critical applications like video conferencing, and dynamic weighted bonding, which optimizes the use of diverse connections with varying speeds. These settings help maintain consistent performance for both real-time streaming and large file uploads, making it easier for users to operate without needing extensive IT support in the field.

## Document_20

Peplink's SpeedFusion is a core product that enables the establishment of multiple VPN tunnels directly to clients' infrastructure, allowing for flexible management of voice services and other resources. The deployment strategies for SpeedFusion can vary, with options for self-hosted infrastructure or SpeedFusion Cloud, each catering to different client needs. The use of public IPs from data centers facilitates seamless reconnections for clients in case of disruptions. SpeedFusion can complement existing IPsec setups by providing a more seamless failover experience. Additionally, InControl2 offers enhanced remote management capabilities, allowing administrators to access devices behind Peplink routers without the need for separate management networks, thus improving operational efficiency and reducing the need for on-site visits.

## Document_21

Peplink's SpeedFusion technology allows users to combine multiple internet connections for improved reliability and performance, with a simplified setup process requiring only a few clicks. Users can configure networks to utilize load balancing or SpeedFusion based on their specific needs, such as streaming or work calls. The latest firmware (8.4) includes native support for Starlink, enabling monitoring through the InControl2 cloud management system. Starlink's high-performance flat mount dish offers advantages over the standard dish, including better speed and performance in obstructed environments. Users can connect various WAN sources, including Starlink, cable modems, and cellular networks, to optimize their internet connectivity. Tools like coverage mapping apps can assist users in evaluating cellular coverage in new locations, while Peplink devices enhance connectivity options for mobile users.

## Document_22

The Peplink system allows users to manage multiple internet connections, including Starlink and various cellular options like T-Mobile and AT&T, providing a seamless experience while traveling. The admin console displays active connections and their performance metrics, including speed tests and latency, enabling users to assess the health of each connection. The system supports SpeedFusion technology, which enhances connection reliability and speed by aggregating multiple links. Users can easily switch between connections based on performance, and all devices connect to a single Wi-Fi source, simplifying network management. The setup allows for flexibility in connection choices, ensuring consistent internet access even in varying conditions, such as when under trees or in campgrounds.

## Document_23

Peplink's SpeedFusion technology creates a VPN tunnel from a device to a data center, allowing for reliable internet connectivity, particularly for mission-critical applications like VoIP and video calls. However, it can interfere with streaming services like Netflix due to location-based content restrictions. Users can set up separate networks to bypass the VPN for specific devices. Peplink routers utilize load balancing across multiple WAN connections, which can lead to inconsistent performance if some connections are unreliable. Users should regularly test connection speeds to ensure optimal performance. The setup can include a SIM injector for easy SIM card management and can operate on 12 volts, eliminating the need for an inverter for certain components, although Starlink requires 110 volts. The integration of cellular modems and Starlink provides flexibility in connectivity options for mobile setups.

## Document_24

SpeedFusion is a feature that allows the bonding of multiple WAN sources into a single, more reliable internet connection via a VPN tunnel. The device discussed supports multiple connections, including two cellular modems, a WAN port for wired connections like Starlink, a USB port for additional 5G modems, and Wi-Fi WAN for public Wi-Fi. It operates on a uniform operating system, currently version 8.2, which receives regular updates for features and security. The device also supports remote management through InControl, which provides insights into WAN health and data usage. Additionally, there are options for direct wire DC power kits and a six-port fuse box for organized power management in mobile installations, enhancing the installation experience for multiple devices.

## Document_25

For a work from home setup requiring multiple WAN connections, the Peplink Balance 20X is recommended as a suitable router. It features a built-in CAT4 modem and the option to add a pluggable CAT12 modem module for higher LTE speeds. The router supports one Ethernet WAN port and a USB WAN for additional connectivity. Utilizing SpeedFusion cloud profiles allows for directing VoIP and Zoom traffic through a bonded tunnel while managing other internet usage through the main WAN. Additionally, the Balance 20X includes a built-in AP controller for managing access points, with centralized management available through an inControl2 subscription included in the prime care license for the first year.

## Document_26

For a work from home setup requiring reliable internet for VoIP and video calls, a Peplink Balance 20X is a suitable option, particularly for bonding multiple WAN connections such as Starlink, DSL, and AT&T LTE. The Balance 30 LTE and 580X are also considered, with the latter allowing for extensive WAN options including DSL, Starlink, and multiple cellular connections. The use of HD2 dome antennas is suggested for improved cellular signal, especially when mounted on the roof, to enhance connectivity and performance.

## Document_27

For a work from home setup requiring a router with 3 WAN capabilities, including Starlink, DSL, and AT&T LTE, Peplink offers several models suitable for bonding connections to ensure reliable VoIP and Zoom calls without drops. The comparison link provided leads to specific Peplink Balance models that can meet these requirements.

## Document_28

For optimal performance over a SpeedFusion/PepVPN tunnel using Starlink, it is important that the far end of the tunnel has sufficient bandwidth to support the connection.

## Document_29

The best recorded performance over a SpeedFusion/PepVPN tunnel using Starlink is 69 Mbps, with typical speeds observed in the 20 Mbps range.

## Document_30

SpeedFusion can be configured to use hot failover, allowing traffic to be routed through a WISP connection only when the Starlink connection is down. This setup can maintain VoIP sessions and client VPN connections during outages. Users have reported frequent brief outages with Starlink, making it necessary to have a backup connection like WISP or 4G for reliability.

## Document_31

To utilize SpeedFusion for bonding connections while prioritizing Starlink over a WISP connection, it is possible to configure the setup to route all traffic through Starlink unless it is down, at which point the WISP connection can be used. This configuration is beneficial for maintaining bandwidth efficiency, especially since the WISP service is bandwidth limited.

## Document_32

To improve VPN and VOIP connection stability while using Starlink and a WISP connection with a Pepwave Surf SOHO, it is possible to configure SpeedFusion to bond the connections. However, it is important to note that WAN smoothing may need to be disabled if experiencing disconnections, as it can affect connection stability. The goal is to route traffic primarily through the Starlink connection and only utilize the WISP connection when Starlink is down, due to the bandwidth limitations of the WISP service.

## Document_33

To improve VPN and VOIP connections while using Starlink and a WISP connection with a Peplink router, it is possible to configure SpeedFusion to bond the connections and set it up to route traffic through the WISP connection only when Starlink is down. Additionally, adjusting the Health Check Method on the WiFi WAN connection may enhance the detection of failures, potentially reducing disconnections during Starlink outages.

## Document_34

To configure SpeedFusion for bonding connections while prioritizing a WISP connection only when Starlink is down, one can set health checks with specific parameters to monitor the Starlink connection. The recommended settings include a health check with 3 failures and a 4-second TTL every 5 seconds, with recovery on 1 good check. The outbound policy should prioritize Starlink for normal traffic and switch to LTE when the health check fails. For high availability applications like Zoom and VPN, a separate outbound policy can be created to prioritize SpeedFusion, then Starlink, and finally LTE, with WAN smoothing set to Normal and FEC set to Low. This setup may still result in some audio issues during outages, indicating the need for further adjustments.

## Document_35

To utilize SpeedFusion effectively with a WISP connection and Starlink, it is possible to configure SpeedFusion to bond the connections while routing traffic through the WISP connection only when Starlink is down. This setup is beneficial for managing bandwidth limitations of the WISP service. Additionally, tools like Tcpdump or Wireshark can help identify main DNS domains for applications like Zoom and Webex, which may be relevant for ensuring proper connectivity and performance.

This setup allows traffic to be routed through the WISP connection only when the Starlink connection is down, which is beneficial for managing bandwidth limitations of the WISP service.

Synergy Mode, introduced in Firmware 8.3.0, allows multiple Peplink devices to be cascaded, combining their WANs into a single virtual interface on a Synergy Controller. The Synergized Device acts as a modem or client without management options, while the Synergy Controller manages all WAN interfaces, including Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and Cellular. To enable Synergy Mode, both devices must run the same firmware version, and the Synergy Controller requires an active Care Plan. The Synergized Device can be any compatible model from the Balance, MAX, or UBR series, while the Synergy Controller can be from the X, Balance, MAX, or UBR series. The setup involves connecting the devices correctly and enabling the Synergy Controller in the settings, allowing centralized management of WAN links from the Synergized Device.

Peplink Synergy mode allows multiple routers to function as a single unit, requiring one Peplink router with an active care plan to serve as the Synergy controller. Secondary routers, known as Synergy devices, can connect to this controller, with the first device not needing a care plan while subsequent devices do. The connection between these routers is termed the synergized link. For successful setup, all devices must run firmware version 8.3.0, and the Synergy controller must have at least one active WAN connection. The Synergy device must be reset to factory settings after upgrading to the required firmware. The Synergy mode is enabled through the network tab on the controller's web admin interface, and after configuration, the devices will synchronize, allowing management of WAN connections from the controller. Access to the Synergy device can be obtained through the controller's dashboard, using the same admin credentials as the controller.

In Firmware 7.10 and earlier, a Trunk port would present the default LAN (typically the DATA VLAN) as untagged while other VLANs would be tagged. In a Peplink Balance 20 router, when a port is set to Access type, outbound frames leaving the router on that port are tagged with the defined VLAN (e.g., VLAN=44). For inbound frames, if a frame is tagged with VLAN=44, it is accepted; if it is tagged with a different VLAN, it is dropped; and if it is untagged, it is assigned the VLAN of the Access port. When the port type is set to Trunk, the behavior changes: the Trunk port expects VLAN tags and will drop any untagged frames or frames with VLANs that do not match the trunk configuration. Access ports automatically tag incoming packets, while Trunk ports require existing tags to process packets correctly.

In a Peplink Balance 20 router, when a port is set as an Access port for a defined VLAN (e.g., VLAN 44), outbound frames leaving the router on that port are tagged with VLAN 44 to ensure they are not dropped by downstream switches. For inbound frames, if they are tagged with VLAN 44, they will also be accepted and processed as such. If an inbound frame is tagged with a different VLAN, it will be dropped unless the VLAN is configured to be allowed. Untagged frames will be treated as VLAN 44 if the Access port is configured for that VLAN. When the port type is set to Trunk, it allows multiple VLANs to traverse, and frames will be passed along based on the VLAN configuration; tagged frames will be allowed if they match the trunk configuration, while untagged frames will be allowed if the untagged VLAN is included in the trunk configuration. A general guideline is to use Trunk ports for devices that tag packets and Access ports for those that do not.

query: Which prerequisites must be met, what setup procedures should be followed, and what operational aspects need attention when installing a Wi-Fi Mesh network utilizing Peplink or Pepwave equipment, and in this context, how is VLAN tagged SSID support implemented and utilized within the mesh?
answer: To deploy a Wi-Fi Mesh network with Peplink or Pepwave devices, you must have a compatible router or access point (AP) with 802.11ac or newer Wi-Fi, and you need to ensure that all devices are running firmware that supports mesh features—specifically, firmware version 8.1.1 or newer for routers and versions 3.6.2, 3.7.3, or 3.8.1 for APs. Each mesh AP must be powered, despite being wirelessly connected. The setup process involves creating a Mesh Profile in the router and AP settings, assigning matching Mesh IDs and keys across all devices, and enabling the profile. If using an AP Controller, this can streamline the provisioning and deployment of mesh settings and SSIDs to all APs. Mesh APs should be strategically placed between the wired AP and the coverage area to ensure strong wireless links, as direct wired APs will always outperform mesh APs due to shared frequencies and radios, which can limit capacity. The mesh operates as a Layer 2 network, allowing VLAN tagged SSIDs to function as they would on a wired network, enabling seamless VLAN management and isolation across the wireless mesh.

query: Which necessary procedures and possible challenges should be considered when connecting two distinct LANs via a Pepwave B380 and B210, taking into account configuration of routing, NAT, firewall, and gateway settings?
answer: To bridge two separate LANs using a Pepwave B380 and B210, start by configuring a static route on the B380 for the secondary LAN's subnet (e.g., 198.42.232.0/24) pointing to the B210's WAN1 IP address (e.g., 198.42.231.242). On the B210, ensure that WAN1 is connected to the primary LAN and that its LAN interface provides DHCP for the secondary LAN subnet. NAT should be disabled and IP forwarding enabled on the B210 to allow direct traffic flow from the primary to the secondary LAN. The firewall rules on both routers must allow traffic between the two subnets. Devices on the primary LAN should use the B380 as their gateway. However, communication from LAN A (primary) to LAN B (secondary) may fail if the B210 has NAT enabled or if the static route or firewall rules are misconfigured. Additionally, intermediary devices like firewall appliances (e.g., Untangle) between the B380 and the LAN may block traffic and need to be configured to permit access to the secondary LAN. In some cases, direct communication may only work if the device's gateway is set to the B210's WAN1 IP, indicating a routing or firewall issue on the B380. If issues persist, use diagnostics like ping and traceroute to identify where the connectivity breaks down.

## Document_1

Peplink's high availability (HA) feature operates on a master/slave architecture, where one router is designated as the master and the other as a backup. The backup router remains inactive while the master is operational, only becoming active if the master fails. This implementation does not support a peer-to-peer relationship where both routers can independently manage their own WANs and VLANs while providing backup for each other. The HA configuration requires synchronization of settings between the master and slave, which is optional but necessary for the slave to be prepared for activation in case of a master failure. If synchronization is not enabled, the slave must be manually configured to match the master.

## Document_2

In a high availability (HA) setup for Peplink Balance routers in NAT mode, the LAN configuration requires a Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) setup with a virtual IP (VIP) for the master and slave units. For the WAN configuration, two options are presented. Option 1 requires three VRRP groups: one for the LAN and one for each ISP, necessitating a total of six public IP addresses. Option 2 suggests a simpler configuration with only two public IP addresses, where the master unit handles both WAN connections and the slave unit takes over the WAN IP address upon failover. The WAN setup involves two ISPs, each with its own subnet and gateway.

## Document_3

Pepwave routers support high availability configurations using the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) as defined in RFC 3768, allowing for redundancy and failover in a master-slave arrangement. In this configuration, two Pepwave routers communicate over the LAN using VRRP, broadcasting heartbeat signals at a frequency of one per second. If the master router fails to send a heartbeat signal for 3 seconds or longer, the slave router activates, initiates WAN connections, and binds to a preconfigured LAN IP address. Upon recovery, the master router will regain its active status by default.

## Document_4

To implement a 1+1 Backup using Peplink Balance devices or MAX 700/HD, both devices must operate in active-standby mode, utilizing High Availability (HA) failover based on Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP). The master device sends periodic VRRP advertisement packets to a multicast address, and the slave device takes over if these packets are not received within a specified interval. Both devices must be on the same subnet and share the same HA group identifier. The configuration requires setting a virtual IP (VIP) as the default gateway for LAN hosts, and additional Ethernet switches are recommended to avoid a single point of failure. Configuration Sync can be enabled for the slave unit to automatically apply changes from the master unit, or the slave can be configured manually using an exported configuration file. The failover process typically takes 10-15 seconds, and both devices should be connected to the Internet in the same mode (NAT or Drop-in).

## Document_13

High availability mode on Peplink routers, also known as Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP), allows for seamless failover between two routers configured in master and slave mode. In this setup, one router (the master) handles all connectivity, while the other (the slave) remains on standby. If the master router experiences a failure, the slave router automatically takes over within approximately 15 seconds, ensuring continuous internet connectivity. The demonstration involved two Peplink Balance 380 routers, with an active ping to Google's public DNS to monitor connectivity. When the master router was turned off, the pings stopped, but once the slave router assumed master status, the pings resumed, demonstrating the effectiveness of the high availability setup. The process also includes the ability for the master router to regain control once it is powered back on, reverting the roles of the routers accordingly.

## Document_14

High Availability (HA) mode, also known as HA mode, provides hardware redundancy by allowing a slave unit to take over the role of a master unit in the event of a failure. This failover mechanism is based on the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP), which sends a heartbeat signal from the master device to the slave device. If the heartbeat is lost due to hardware failure or disconnection, the slave unit assumes the master role. The setup involves configuring two Peplink Balance 20X devices, where the master device is set up first by enabling HA mode, selecting the master role, and configuring a virtual IP address that serves as the default gateway for connected hosts. The slave device is then configured to sync its settings with the master either automatically or manually, ensuring it has a different LAN IP address. The failover process typically takes 10 to 15 seconds, during which all line connections are re-established. Successful configuration can be verified through the web admin dashboard of the slave device, which will indicate that HA mode is enabled.

## Document_15

The high availability feature of the Peplink Balance 20X can cause issues with cable modems, particularly those from Comcast, due to the changing of the Ethernet MAC address on the WAN port. This can lead to the modem becoming unresponsive, as it is sensitive to MAC address changes. The MAC address used during high availability is an unassigned IANA MAC address (00:00:5e:01:01:fa), which is not appropriate for this function. The expected virtual MAC address for VRRP should be 00:00:5e:00:01:fa. When high availability is enabled, the WAN port may show a private IP address instead of the public IP, and the WAN status may indicate down due to DNS test failures, suggesting that the modem is not passing traffic from the router. Packet captures during this time may yield unexpected results, such as capturing LAN traffic instead of WAN traffic.

This means that only one public IP address is needed for the HA setup, as the slave router will take over the master router's public IP address upon failure, rather than requiring multiple public IP addresses for each router.

query: In a NAT-mode setup, how does Peplink's High Availability (HA) functionality leveraging VRRP provide uninterrupted failover between the primary (master) and backup (slave) routers, and what are the main steps and important factors to consider when configuring it, particularly with regard to virtual IP usage, configuration synchronization, and network switch configuration?
answer: Peplink’s High Availability (HA) feature uses a master/slave architecture based on the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) to provide hardware redundancy and seamless failover. In this setup, the master router handles all LAN and WAN traffic while periodically sending VRRP advertisement (heartbeat) packets to the slave. If the slave does not receive these packets within a specified interval (typically 3 seconds), it automatically assumes the master’s role, taking over WAN and LAN responsibilities in about 10–15 seconds. The virtual IP (VIP) is a critical component, serving as the default gateway for all LAN hosts so that failover is transparent to end devices. Both routers must be on the same subnet and share the same HA group identifier. Configuration Sync can be enabled to automatically synchronize settings from the master to the slave every five minutes, or the slave can be configured manually. For resilience, additional Ethernet switches are recommended to avoid a single point of failure. In NAT mode, the VIP must be set as the default gateway for all LAN hosts, and both routers should be connected to the internet in NAT mode for proper operation.

To establish a SpeedFusion tunnel, two devices are required: a host with a static IP and an endpoint with a dynamic IP. The setup involves configuring the SpeedFusion VPN settings through InControl2, ensuring firmware is updated to at least version 8.3.0. It features automatic failover capabilities, ensuring continuous connectivity even during outages. ## Document_2

OpenVPN licenses for Pepwave routers are not transferable and must be generated based on the unique serial number of each device.

## Document_3

The IMEI number for the Pepwave Max BR1 mini LTEA can be found through InControl2 by clicking on details under the cellular section, as well as directly in the web admin interface under the cellular details on the main page.

## Document_4

To configure a UBR router with two SIM cards for specific traffic routing, create two outbound policy rules. The first rule should direct WiFi traffic through the AT&T SIM card by specifying the source as the WiFi network. The second rule should cover the entire LAN network range (192.168.50.0/24) to route all other traffic, such as that from devices connected via Ethernet, through the Verizon SIM card. Ensure that the WiFi rule is prioritized at the top of the policy list to take precedence over the LAN rule.

## Document_5

To prevent frequent logouts from the Pepwave router's web GUI, users can adjust a setting that controls the session timeout duration. For example, on a Balance router, this setting can be configured to not log the user out for six hours, and similar options are available for MAX devices.

## Document_6

A recent firmware version 8.1.2s052 for the Surf SOHO MK3 has been released, which may address connectivity issues experienced by devices that suddenly cannot see the SSID while others can. The firmware is available for download on the Peplink website, although no specific Release Notes are provided for this version.

## Document_7

The correct cable for the power port in question is identified by the part number ACW-638, which can be purchased through certified partners.

## Document_8

To use the Device API with a username and password for accessing the Pepwave router's status, refer to the latest device level API documentation available in the software supplements on the Peplink website. This documentation will provide guidance on how to properly authenticate and generate an access token for API access.

## Document_9

To resolve issues with a router losing connection and not broadcasting its SSID, it is recommended to upgrade the firmware from version 8.0.0 build 1429 to 8.0.2. If the problem persists after the upgrade, it is advisable to log a ticket with engineering for further assistance.

## Document_10

Pepwave products do not use Broadcom or Cypress Wi-Fi chipsets, and therefore, they are not affected by the CVE-2019-15126 security flaw that allows a bad actor to exploit encrypted Wi-Fi connections by changing the key to zero, resulting in unencrypted Wi-Fi.

## Document_11

To find the IMEI number for a Pepwave Balance 30 LTE, log into the device's interface and click on the details section for the cellular settings, where the IMEI number will be displayed.

## Document_12

The Pepwave MAX device can be configured with a DHCP scope that technically has no limit, but it is rated for up to 60 users. However, connecting that many users to a single cellular connection may negatively impact the overall user experience.

## Document_13

The IMEI of a cellular device can be found in the Dashboard of the Pepwave router by clicking on the "Details" link for the Cellular connection, which displays the IMEI in a pop-up window.

## Document_14

To modify the bandwidth allowance settings for a cellular connection using the API, the 'sim' parameter must be formatted as an array. The correct structure includes an 'id' for the SIM and the 'bandwidthAllowanceMonitor' settings, which should include 'enable', 'start', and 'monthlyAllowance' with 'value' and 'unit'.

## Document_15

If a Pepwave Max BR1 MK2 is intermittently failing to broadcast its SSID, it may be due to the broadcasted Wi-Fi channel not being supported by the Wi-Fi client. Adjusting the Wi-Fi channel settings in the AP > Settings section may resolve the issue.

## Document_16

When downloading a configuration file from a Pepwave MAX Transit, the device name and device ID are included, which can lead to conflicts in VPN tunnels due to identical device IDs across multiple devices. Currently, there is no option to exclude the local ID from the configuration file, and the ability to change the local ID is not available in the device settings. The ICA software version mentioned is 2.8.2.6, which may be outdated.

## Document_17

To reserve fixed bandwidth for a specific device using a Pepwave MAX BR1, it is necessary to use Quality of Service (QoS) settings. However, creating user groups for QoS requires defining the upload and download speeds of the connection, which is not possible with a cellular connection.

## Document_18

The MAX HD4 can load balance sessions over WAN connections independently. However, using a SpeedFusion VPN terminated to a Balance router at the other end enables the bonding of WAN connections at a packet level, which provides session persistence and increases bandwidth.

## Document_19

The MAX HD4 can load balance across up to 4 cellular links, which is suitable for increasing bandwidth for multiple users. However, to bond two or more cellular connections into a single session for higher bandwidth, such as for a file download or video stream, SpeedFusion bonding is required along with another device to manage the bonded traffic.

## Document_20

In a fleet of vehicles using BR1 devices, it is normal for the devices to perform DNS inquiries every two seconds as part of the health check behavior, which uses DNS inquiry as the default method. These settings can be adjusted through the Details tab of the cellular connection.

## Document_21

The MAX HD2 router can bond multiple cellular connections, specifically Cell #1 and Cell #2, as well as Cell #3 and Cell #4. This bonding capability may help in addressing issues related to cellular dropouts by providing redundancy and improved reliability in the connection.

## Document_22

To access a Pepwave router when the default IP address (192.168.50.1) is not working, connect a device directly to the router and check the device's network properties to find the gateway IP address, which will be the router's IP. Alternatively, registering the device with InControl and using remote web admin can provide access to the router settings.

## Document_23

To use a Pepwave GTO to provide an Ethernet port for a non-wireless enabled laptop via a Verizon Jetpack 4G LTE, the GTO should be set up in Cellular Mode on the dashboard. Additionally, the Jetpack must be configured in tethered mode before connecting it to the GTO. Checking the dashboard for messages after connecting the Jetpack can help diagnose any issues.

## Document_24

In the Pepwave Surf OTG, the 'Profile select' feature is intended for editing profiles rather than indicating the currently active profile. The device automatically selects the most suitable profile from the list to connect to the available Access Points, which may not necessarily be the last created profile. There are plans to improve the web UI to display the currently connected profile on the setup page in a future release.

## Document_25

For users of the Pepwave MAX Transit DUO seeking alternative cellular connections, it has been noted that Visible can work effectively when the APN is changed. This suggests that users may find success with Visible as a data plan option, despite initial compatibility issues with other carriers.

## Document_26

A user successfully signed up for the AT&T 100GB Prepaid plan by providing the IMEI number of their device at an AT&T store, which allowed them to activate the service on their Pepwave router. Additionally, online activation was confirmed to work on a Pepwave BR1 IP67 model.

## Document_27

To move a device from one group to another within InControl, navigate to the Group Dashboard page, click on Manage, select the device by ticking the corresponding box, and then use the Actions pull-down menu to select Move.

## Document_28

query: What are the necessary steps and recommended approaches to establish robust, high-bandwidth bonded internet using Peplink/Pepwave MAX routers like the MAX 700 or HD2 with several modems, and how do SpeedFusion VPN and FusionHub contribute to such configurations, particularly for applications like streaming or disaster recovery?
answer:
To achieve reliable, high-throughput bonded internet connectivity with Peplink/Pepwave MAX devices like the MAX 700 or HD2 using multiple modems, several requirements and best practices should be followed:

1. Use SpeedFusion VPN Bonding technology to aggregate bandwidth from multiple SIM cards, USB modems, or WAN sources. This allows for the creation of a single, high-capacity connection suitable for demanding applications such as streaming or disaster recovery.

2. For true bonding (as opposed to simple load balancing), you must deploy two SpeedFusion-capable devices: one at the remote/mobile site (e.g., MAX 700 or HD2) and another at a fixed endpoint. The endpoint can be a physical Peplink Balance router or a virtual appliance called FusionHub, which can be hosted in the cloud or datacenter. This setup enables packet-level breakdown and reassembly across all available WAN links.

3. When using FusionHub, ensure it has sufficient WAN bandwidth to match or exceed the total bandwidth being bonded. FusionHub is essential for scenarios where a cloud-based endpoint is required, such as public streaming to platforms like Facebook Live.

4. For point-to-point bonded links (e.g., between a central storage server and a disaster recovery server), two MAX 700 units can be used, even with dynamic public IP addresses, by leveraging Dynamic DNS services for addressing and maintaining the VPN tunnel.

5. Avoid including high-latency connections in the bonding pool, as they can degrade the performance of the bonded link.

6. Bandwidth management features on MAX devices can be used to reserve or cap bandwidth for individual clients, optimizing distribution and performance, but these limitations are applied per IP and not by application type.

7. For streaming or similar applications, having a stable public-facing IP address on the SpeedFusion endpoint is often required. This is achievable with either a physical Balance router or FusionHub.

8. SpeedFusion can work with dynamic IPs as long as Dynamic DNS is configured, enabling connectivity even in mobile or changing network environments.

Following these best practices ensures the bonded connection is robust, high-performing, and suitable for critical use cases like streaming or disaster recovery.

query: In what ways do the Pepwave Max BR1 Mini Cat 6, Max BR1 Pro 5G, and Max BR1 Pro Cat 20 LTE differ regarding supported carriers, modem class, Wi-Fi features, data throughput, and antenna setup?
answer:
The Pepwave Max BR1 Mini Cat 6 is compatible with all major carriers (AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, and Canadian carriers), features a Cat 6 modem with carrier aggregation (up to 2 bands), and supports dual-band Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz) when the failover license is activated. Its theoretical throughput is 300 Mbps download and 50 Mbps upload. The device comes with two cellular antennas, two Wi-Fi antennas, and a GPS receiver.

The Max BR1 Pro 5G and Max BR1 Pro Cat 20 LTE share the same hardware form factor, but the 5G model includes a 5G modem (backward compatible with 4G LTE), while the Cat 20 is limited to 4G LTE. Both support all major carriers and updated bands, including band 71. The Cat 20 model achieves 2 Gbps download and 150 Mbps upload, while the 5G model can reach 2 Gbps download and 700 Mbps upload. Both support five times carrier aggregation for download and three times for upload, and feature advanced Wi-Fi 6 (dual-band 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz) for improved speed and range. Each model includes four cellular antennas and two Wi-Fi antennas, supporting MIMO technology for better data transmission and security with military-grade encryption.

query: What restrictions does the Pepwave BR1 Mini LTE have when it comes to SIM bonding, and which other solutions or technologies does Peplink provide for users needing multi-SIM or aggregated connections to achieve greater bandwidth?
answer: The Pepwave BR1 Mini LTE does not support true SIM bonding because it has only one LTE radio and cannot aggregate bandwidth from multiple SIM cards. Devices that support SpeedFusion, such as the Peplink Compact Dual 4G LTE Mobile Router, are suitable alternatives for achieving multi-SIM bonded connectivity. For establishing a site-to-site connection between Peplink devices, it is recommended to use PepVPN/SpeedFusion instead of IPSec VPN, as IPSec can have issues with NAT. PepVPN/SpeedFusion is designed to handle NAT traversal effectively, allowing for seamless connectivity across NAT environments.

## Document_2

To change the internal IP address for remote access on a PEPLink router GS-B20, log in to the web admin interface, navigate to Network > Inbound Access : Port Forwarding, and update the destination IP in the existing port forwarding rule to the new server address (192.168.0.4).

## Document_3

When using L2TP/PPTP on a Peplink Balance 710 with third-party DHCP, connectivity issues arise where remote PCs cannot access LAN resources beyond the Peplink IP. This issue is reproducible on a Balance 380, and while enabling DHCP on the Peplink allows PPTP to function correctly, disabling it and relying on a third-party DHCP server leads to connectivity failures. L2TP VPN clients receive IP addresses within the LAN subnet but can only ping certain hosts, indicating potential routing or firewall issues within the Peplink configuration. It is suggested that activating the Peplink DHCP server for L2TP VPN clients could resolve these issues by assigning IP addresses from a different subnet.

## Document_4

When using a Peplink Balance 380 with an external DHCP server, L2TP VPN clients may experience connectivity issues to certain hosts within the LAN. While the VPN clients can receive IP addresses from the DHCP server and ping some devices, they cannot reach critical servers like Terminalserver1 and Terminalserver2. It is suggested that having VPN clients receive IP addresses within the same subnet as the LAN may cause routing issues. A potential solution could involve enabling the Peplink DHCP server specifically for L2TP VPN clients to assign them IP addresses from a different subnet, which may improve routing and connectivity.

## Document_5

When using a Peplink device with DHCP disabled, it is possible to connect to the internal PPTP server if the internal Microsoft-based DHCP server is on the native LAN of the Peplink Balance. The current firmware supports this configuration, allowing clients to connect to the PPTP service without the Peplink assigning IP addresses directly.

## Document_6

For clients to connect to the PPTP server built into a Peplink device, the DHCP server on the Peplink must be enabled. If DHCP is disabled on the Peplink, it cannot assign IP addresses to VPN clients, which may prevent them from connecting to the PPTP service.

## Document_7

For site-to-site VPNs between Peplink devices, the options include SpeedFusion, PepVPN, and IPSec. For host-to-network connections from a computer to a Peplink device, the only VPN option available is PPTP. query: In what ways do the DHCP server configurations on a Peplink router influence the ability of PPTP and L2TP VPN clients to connect to LAN resources, and what is the suggested setup to fix access problems when a third-party DHCP server is in use?
answer: When using PPTP or L2TP VPN on a Peplink router, the DHCP server configuration significantly impacts client connectivity to LAN resources. If the Peplink's DHCP server is disabled and a third-party DHCP server assigns IP addresses, VPN clients often experience limited access: they may connect but can only reach the Peplink device itself or a subset of LAN hosts. Enabling the Peplink DHCP server for VPN clients, and assigning them addresses from a different subnet than the main LAN, resolves these routing and connectivity issues. For PPTP, Peplink's DHCP server must be enabled for reliable client-to-LAN connectivity. For L2TP, assigning VPN clients to a separate subnet via the Peplink's DHCP server is recommended to prevent routing conflicts and ensure access to all necessary LAN resources.

The R Link is a new multicarrier data plan from Mobile Must Have that allows users to connect to the top four U.S. carriers (AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, and US Cellular) using a single SIM card and data plan, specifically designed for higher-end Pepwave routers. This plan operates as a mobile virtual network operator (MVNO), providing flexibility and redundancy by automatically switching between carriers based on coverage. The primary offerings include 100 GB for $99 and 300 GB for $159 per month, with options for higher data limits. The plans prioritize traffic, avoiding typical carrier throttles. Additionally, R Link Connect is a preconfigured Pepwave router service that simplifies connectivity for users without existing Pepwave hardware, offering a rental model that allows users to eventually own the router after 12 months. This service includes options for dual modem connections for enhanced redundancy and speed.

The R Link Connect Solo is a new device from R Link Wireless, which operates on all four major US carrier towers: Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile, and US Cellular. It allows users to access multiple networks with a single plan, providing prioritized connectivity for faster speeds. The device includes two antennas—one for Wi-Fi and one for LTE/5G—and is designed for easy setup, with clear labeling to avoid connection errors. Users can expect solid performance, with speeds potentially reaching up to 100 Mbps depending on tower connectivity and network congestion. The device is built for stability and redundancy, ensuring a reliable connection for various online activities. Additional antenna options are available for enhanced reception, including window-mounted and roof-mounted antennas, compatible with R Link Connect devices.

The Solo connects to one tower at a time, available in LTE and 5G versions, while the Duo features dual modems for simultaneous connections, providing redundancy and improved bandwidth. Pricing for the Solo starts at $99, while the Duo starts at $499. Data plans for the Solo include options for 100 GB, 300 GB, and unlimited data, while the Duo offers 500 GB and unlimited plans. Both devices support SpeedFusion technology and are designed for easy integration with existing Peplink hardware, allowing users to maintain connectivity while on the move.

## Document_2

The Peplink Balance 20 can utilize two WAN connections simultaneously and load balance between them using various algorithms. However, this does not equate to bonding in the sense of providing a single connection that combines the speeds of both WANs. For instance, if WAN1 has a speed of 80Mbps and WAN2 has 30Mbps, a single client will be limited to the speed of the faster WAN (80Mbps) unless a more complex bonding solution is implemented to allow the client to utilize the combined speed of both connections (110Mbps).

## Document_3

For configuring a Peplink Balance 20 with eero Pros, users can choose between Double NAT or bridge mode, depending on their preference for utilizing eero features. The Balance 20 has a throughput of 150 Mbps, which may be less than the combined total of multiple WAN connections. For environments with 20-30 users, especially those using bandwidth-intensive applications like Zoom, it may be advisable to consider upgrading to a different Peplink model to accommodate higher throughput needs.

## Document_4

To connect two hotspots (AT&T and Verizon) to a Peplink Balance 20 for maximum upload speeds, configure both WAN connections in Load Balancing & Failover mode. Set both WANs to 'Always-on (Priority 1)' in the WAN settings and ensure the Outbound Policy is set to 'Auto'. You can monitor the status of each WAN under Status -> Active Sessions. For more advanced bonding capabilities, consider upgrading to a Balance 20X and utilizing SpeedFusion technology with a FusionHub Solo or a partner hosting SpeedFusion tunnels.

## Document_5

To connect multiple hotspots to a Peplink device for increased bandwidth and speed, it is important to utilize the Load Balancing & Failover capabilities of the device. For bonding connections from multiple sources, SpeedFusion Cloud can be employed, which allows for the effective use of both AT&T and Verizon hotspots connected via Ethernet to the Peplink device.

query: In what ways does the Peplink Balance 20 handle multiple WAN connections to enhance bandwidth, and how do load balancing and SpeedFusion bonding differ in their usage on the Balance 20 compared to the Balance 20X?
answer: The Peplink Balance 20 manages multiple WAN connections by performing session-based load balancing, distributing sessions across the available WANs to enhance overall bandwidth for multiple users and devices. However, it does not support true bonding—meaning a single session, such as a video stream or file download, will only use the bandwidth of one WAN at a time. Advanced bonding, where multiple WANs are combined to provide a single, faster connection for individual sessions, is only available with SpeedFusion technology, which is not supported on the Balance 20 but is available on the Balance 20X (albeit with a bandwidth cap). The Balance 20X can utilize SpeedFusion Cloud for bonding, but the maximum throughput is limited to 100 Mbps. For basic load balancing (without bonding), both models can increase aggregate bandwidth for multiple sessions, but only the Balance 20X supports SpeedFusion bonding for single-session aggregation, subject to device-specific throughput limits.

## Document_2

For WAN backup configurations on Peplink Balance series and MAX series routers, the health checks for the backup WAN depend on the type of WAN and the product model. For Balance series Ethernet WAN/Fiber, the backup WAN is in a disconnected state (Cold Standby), meaning health checks will not run. For Balance series Mobile Internet WAN/Cellular and MAX series Ethernet/WAN/Cellular/WIFI WAN, the backup WAN can be set to either 'Remain connected (Hot Standby)' or 'Disconnect (Cold Standby)'. If the backup WAN is set to 'Remain Connected', WAN health checks will continue to run, allowing for proactive monitoring of the backup connection. If set to 'Disconnect', health checks will not function, and no traffic can be sent.

## Document_3

In the Peplink Balance series, when a WAN connection is set as a backup, it remains in a disconnected state (Cold Standby), which prevents health checks from being performed on that backup connection. This means that users will not receive alerts regarding issues with the backup WAN until it is needed, highlighting a limitation in the current configuration for monitoring backup connections.

## Document_4

To reduce traffic on a standby WAN connection in a SpeedFusion setup, consider changing the WAN configuration from Hot Standby to Cold Standby. Hot Standby maintains some tunnel connection traffic, which can incur costs, while Cold Standby does not actively send traffic unless it is needed for failover.

## Document_5

To resolve issues with a Pepwave HD4 MBX router incorrectly using cellular connections instead of prioritizing VSAT, switching the cellular connections to Cold Standby mode can ensure that they are only utilized as a failover option when the primary VSAT connection is down. This adjustment resulted in consistent latency of 700ms, which is appropriate for VSAT, indicating that the cellular connections are no longer being used during normal operation unless the VSAT fails.

## Document_6

To validate the idle disconnection mode on a Pepwave BR1, users can check the Dashboard for the status of the modem connection. The modem will deactivate the PDP connection when the idle disconnect timer expires if no internet traffic is detected. The standby state operates differently based on priority settings; if cellular is set as the first priority, it remains connected (Hot Standby) for faster failover, whereas if it is not, it can enter a disconnected state (Cold Standby), which requires more time for failover.

## Document_7

Purchasing used Peplink devices poses risks such as the inability to verify the source or quality, potential illegal acquisition, and possible access to data by previous owners if the device remains registered with them in InControl 2. Users can log in to the device via Web admin using specific IP addresses for MAX and Balance series products, but cannot access InControl 2 if the device is still registered to its original owner. It is recommended to buy Peplink products from certified partners to ensure security and proper registration.

## Document_8

In a SpeedFusion setup with multiple WAN connections, if WAN 1 and WAN 2 are set as active with priority 1 and WAN 3 as standby with priority 6, it is possible to observe traffic on the standby WAN. In this case, the standby WAN is showing approximately 5 kbit/s of traffic, which may incur costs if the connection is metered. To manage this traffic, users may need to explore options to lower or eliminate usage on the standby WAN.

## Document_9

In a setup with a Peplink HD4 MBX using 4 cellular connections and 1 VSAT line, if the VSAT is set as priority 1 and cellular connections as priority 2, the cellular links may still be utilized for health checks even when in standby mode. To prevent cellular connections from being used for data when in standby, their state can be set to 'Disconnected'. The behavior observed in speed tests suggests that the cellular connections might still be active in the SpeedFusion profile, indicating they are not fully in standby as intended.

## Document_10

Purchasing used Peplink devices poses risks such as the inability to verify the source or quality, potential registration with a previous owner, and possible access to data by that owner. If a used device is still registered with its previous owner, the new owner cannot access InControl 2, as Peplink cannot change registrations due to security and privacy concerns. However, configuration can still be done via web admin using specific IP addresses for MAX and Balance series products. It is recommended to buy Peplink devices from certified partners to avoid these issues.

query: What impact does changing a backup WAN connection from Hot Standby to Cold Standby mode have on WAN health checks, costs related to standby traffic, and failover efficiency on Peplink Balance and MAX series routers, especially within multi-WAN or SpeedFusion configurations?
answer: Switching a backup WAN to Hot Standby mode keeps the connection active and enables continuous WAN health checks, which allows for proactive monitoring and faster failover. However, this may result in ongoing background traffic (such as SpeedFusion tunnel keepalives or health checks) even when the WAN is not actively used, potentially incurring costs on metered connections. In contrast, setting a backup WAN to Cold Standby disconnects the link, disabling health checks and eliminating standby traffic costs, but this also means that the connection will take longer to become active during failover and users will not be alerted to issues with the backup WAN until it is needed. In multi-WAN or SpeedFusion setups, Hot Standby can cause unexpected standby WAN usage (such as a few kbit/s of tunnel or health check traffic), while Cold Standby ensures that standby WANs are only used when primary links fail, preventing unnecessary costs and guaranteeing that only the prioritized WAN is used during normal operation.

For general load balancing, the weighted balance algorithm should be used.
Weights should be assigned according to each WAN's speed to distribute sessions proportionally.
An example weight ratio is 3:2 for 3Mbps and 2Mbps WANs.
For specific traffic types like HTTPS or Skype, custom rules can prioritize one WAN over the other using Priority or Overflow algorithms.
Rules are processed top-to-bottom in the configuration.
Specific application rules should be placed above general rules.
Health checks must be enabled to ensure failover works.
If the primary WAN fails, traffic is directed to the next available WAN.
Technicians can specify rules by protocol, port, or source IP to direct certain workstations or applications through a preferred WAN.
Adjusting upload and download bandwidth settings in the WAN configuration refines which WAN is preferred for active traffic.
Using weighted balancing for general use, specific rules for critical applications, and health check-based failover ensures optimal bandwidth utilization, prioritization, and reliability.

SpeedFusion requires a VPN connection because standard internet connections do not support features like hot failover, WAN smoothing, or bonding in a conventional manner. ## Document_3

For establishing a site-to-site connection between Peplink devices, it is recommended to use PepVPN/SpeedFusion instead of IPSec VPN, as IPSec can have issues with NAT. PepVPN/SpeedFusion is designed to handle NAT traversal effectively, allowing for seamless connectivity across NAT environments.

Additionally, SpeedFusion allows for bonding multiple WAN links, enabling aggregate bandwidth between the sites.

For site-to-site VPN configurations involving Peplink devices, using SpeedFusion VPN is recommended over traditional IPSec due to its ability to maintain VPN connections during WAN failures and to aggregate bandwidth from multiple WAN connections. SpeedFusion provides military-grade 256-bit AES encryption for data security and is noted for its ease of setup. The conversation also highlights issues with double NAT and private IP addresses in the context of VPN configurations, particularly with Cisco ASA and Peplink devices.

## Document_10

## Document_11

SpeedFusion allows for bonding multiple WAN links by sending packets down each link in a round robin fashion, with the ability to stop using a link if it experiences poor performance. The Dynamic Weighted Bonding (DWB) algorithm measures response times on each link to estimate available bandwidth and dynamically assigns weights to optimize throughput based on latency changes. This approach aims to utilize the least congested links more effectively, contrasting with the standard bonding method that fills both links equally.

## Document_12

SpeedFusion is a point-to-point VPN technology that requires at least two devices to create a bonded VPN using multiple WAN connections. ## Document_13

SpeedFusion technology allows for the combination of multiple WAN connections to enhance internet speed and reliability. It operates on a hierarchy where PepVPN serves as the foundation, followed by SpeedFusion Hot Failover and then SpeedFusion Bonding. WAN Smoothing can be enabled to duplicate packets for reduced packet loss, consuming additional bandwidth. If WAN Smoothing is set to maximum, the SpeedFusion distribution algorithm is ignored, but at lower levels, duplicate packets are distributed according to the selected traffic distribution rules. In scenarios where the Lowest Latency distribution is used, SpeedFusion continuously selects the WAN with the lowest latency for outbound packets, adjusting as network conditions change.

query: In what ways does Peplink SpeedFusion facilitate dependable, high-bandwidth connections between two locations by leveraging several WAN links, and what technical factors should be taken into account to optimize performance and reduce problems like double NAT, data overhead, and inconsistencies in link quality?
answer: Peplink SpeedFusion enables reliable site-to-site connectivity by creating a bonded VPN tunnel across multiple WAN links, allowing aggregation of bandwidth for higher throughput and providing seamless failover if a WAN link fails. To maximize performance, both sites must use compatible Peplink devices, with at least one having a public IP address. SpeedFusion operates at the packet level, distributing traffic across all available WANs and dynamically adjusting for latency or failure using algorithms like Dynamic Weighted Bonding. However, bonding introduces bandwidth overhead (typically around 20%), reducing effective throughput. For optimal bonding, WAN links should have similar quality (bandwidth and latency) to prevent algorithm inefficiency or fluctuating throughput. Double NAT should be avoided, as it complicates VPN setup and may cause peer ID mismatches; ideally, at least one endpoint should have a public or publicly accessible IP. SpeedFusion can operate with or without encryption, allowing for reduced CPU overhead if security is not a priority. Outbound policies can further optimize traffic routing. Using built-in tools and monitoring packet loss, latency, and fragmentation is important for diagnosing and tuning performance. For large deployments, ensure the head-end hardware can handle the aggregate bandwidth, and consider using FusionHub or SpeedFusion Cloud for flexible topologies or remote access.

## Document_1

Peplink's high availability (HA) feature operates on a master/slave architecture, where one router is designated as the master and the other as a backup. The backup router remains inactive while the master is operational, only becoming active if the master fails. This implementation does not support a peer-to-peer relationship where both routers can independently manage their own WANs and VLANs while providing backup for each other. The HA configuration requires synchronization of settings between the master and slave, which is optional but necessary for the slave to be prepared for activation in case of a master failure. If synchronization is not enabled, the slave must be manually configured to match the master.

## Document_2

In a high availability (HA) setup using Peplink Balance routers in NAT mode, VRRP is utilized for WAN as well as LAN configurations. When properly configured, VRRP allows for the transfer of WAN addresses from the master router to the slave router in the event of a failure. This means that only one public IP address is needed for the HA setup, as the slave router will take over the master router's public IP address upon failure, rather than requiring multiple public IP addresses for each router.

## Document_3

In a high availability (HA) setup for Peplink Balance routers in NAT mode, the LAN configuration requires a Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) setup with a virtual IP (VIP) for the master and slave units. For the WAN configuration, two options are presented. Option 1 requires three VRRP groups: one for the LAN and one for each ISP, necessitating a total of six public IP addresses. Option 2 suggests a simpler configuration with only two public IP addresses, where the master unit handles both WAN connections and the slave unit takes over the WAN IP address upon failover. The WAN setup involves two ISPs, each with its own subnet and gateway.

In a High Availability (HA) setup using two Peplink Balance 380 routers configured with VRRP, issues may arise when both routers compete for the master role, particularly during internet connectivity loss. This can lead to network downtime as the routers transition between master and slave roles. The VRRP protocol relies on periodic advertisement packets sent from the master device to maintain the master-slave relationship. If both routers remain connected to the LAN and are aware of each other's WAN connectivity, conflicts over the master role can occur, especially if one router fails to recognize the recovery of the other after a power cycle. Proper diagnostics and physical connection details are crucial for troubleshooting these issues effectively.

## Document_5

Pepwave routers support high availability configurations using the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) as defined in RFC 3768, allowing for redundancy and failover in a master-slave arrangement. In this configuration, two Pepwave routers communicate over the LAN using VRRP, broadcasting heartbeat signals at a frequency of one per second. If the master router fails to send a heartbeat signal for 3 seconds or longer, the slave router activates, initiates WAN connections, and binds to a preconfigured LAN IP address. Upon recovery, the master router will regain its active status by default.
